title: Localized control of large ion crystals in a Penning trap using a spatial light modulator
comment: Main text: 5 pages, 3 figures; End matter: 2 pages, 2 figures; Supplemental material: 10 pages, 11 figures
summary: Penning ion traps as quantum platforms have primarily utilized global control and symmetric Dicke states for quantum simulation and sensing experiments. The introduction of local control greatly increases the power of the platform as a quantum simulator but is technically challenging due to the rapid rotation of the ion crystals. Here we use an ultraviolet-compatible spatial light modulator (SLM) to imprint programmable AC Stark shift patterns with different azimuthal symmetries and gradients that co-rotate with the ion crystals, demonstrating localized coherent control of single plane crystals with greater than 100 ions. Comparisons of the measured ion qubit populations with calculations from independent measurements of the applied AC Stark shift patterns show good agreement, validating the technique and providing a path, with a higher format SLM, for parallelizable, coherent individual ion addressing in Penning traps.

AI.tldr: Researchers demonstrated localized coherent control of over 100 ions in a Penning trap using an UV-compatible spatial light modulator to imprint programmable AC Stark shift patterns that co-rotate with the ion crystals, validated by good agreement between measured qubit populations and calculated shift patterns.
AI.motivation: Penning ion traps lack local control for quantum simulation due to the technical challenge of addressing rapidly rotating ion crystals, limiting their use to global control and symmetric Dicke states.
AI.method: An ultraviolet-compatible spatial light modulator (SLM) was used to imprint programmable AC Stark shift patterns with different azimuthal symmetries and gradients that co-rotate with the ion crystals, enabling localized coherent control.
AI.result: Localized coherent control of single plane crystals with greater than 100 ions was demonstrated, and measured ion qubit populations agreed well with calculations from independent measurements of the applied AC Stark shift patterns.
AI.conclusion: The technique is validated and provides a path, with a higher format SLM, for parallelizable, coherent individual ion addressing in Penning traps.

title: Spin singlets are useful
summary: We evaluate the utility of the spin-zero manifold of an exchange-coupled array of $N$ spins for tasks in quantum computation and quantum simulation. Since pairs of electrons can be readily initialized into a product state of singlets in semiconducting quantum dot arrays, the full spin-zero manifold is available with exchange-only control, providing a Hilbert space of approximate dimension $2^N/(N/2)^{3/2}$, asymptotically close to the $2^N$ dimension of the full spin Hilbert space. Leveraging the spin-zero manifold enables larger computational space in a given array compared to traditional exchange-only control, in which spin arrays are organized into modular units of $n$ spins comprising $N/n$ encoded qubits, limiting to the exponentially smaller Hilbert dimension $2^{N/n}$. Here we focus on benchmarking metrics for this resource utilization by generalizing cross-entropy benchmarking, mirror benchmarking, and out-of-time-ordered correlators to this system. We show that operating in the spin-zero manifold can accelerate the realization of computational quantum advantage applications in semiconductor-based spin qubits.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the utility of the spin-zero manifold of exchange-coupled spin arrays for quantum computation and simulation, showing it provides near-maximal Hilbert space dimension with exchange-only control, and introduces benchmarking metrics to demonstrate its advantage over traditional modular encoding approaches.
AI.motivation: To leverage the spin-zero manifold of exchange-coupled spin arrays to achieve a larger computational Hilbert space (asymptotically close to the full 2^N dimension) compared to traditional exchange-only control with modular encoding, which limits to exponentially smaller Hilbert dimensions.
AI.method: Generalizing cross-entropy benchmarking, mirror benchmarking, and out-of-time-ordered correlators to the spin-zero manifold system for resource utilization benchmarking. The approach uses pairs of electrons initialized into singlet product states in semiconductor quantum dot arrays with exchange-only control.
AI.result: The spin-zero manifold provides a Hilbert space of approximate dimension 2^N/(N/2)^{3/2}, asymptotically close to the full 2^N dimension, whereas traditional exchange-only modular encoding only achieves 2^{N/n} dimension, which is exponentially smaller.
AI.conclusion: Operating in the spin-zero manifold can accelerate the realization of computational quantum advantage applications in semiconductor-based spin qubits.

title: Universal purification dynamics of monitored Clifford circuits
summary: Quantum circuits under sufficiently weak monitoring purify on a timescale $T_P$ exponentially long in the system size. This slowness underlies a universal purification dynamics, whose quantitative description has so far required the replica trick, with a delicate analytic continuation. We show that monitored Clifford circuits on $L$ qudits of prime dimension $q$ bypass this construction entirely: in the scaling limit at fixed $x = t/T_P(L)$, purification reduces to the Markovian decay of the density-matrix rank, an exactly solvable death process descending from infinity. We compute the full scaling functions in compact form: all Rényi entropies collapse onto a universal curve $\langle S(x) \rangle$. Exact stabilizer simulations at $q=2,3,5$ confirm the predictions, with no fitting parameter for the global model and $T_P$ as the only fitted scale for local brick-wall circuits. Also, the replica problem amounts to a tilted version of the same Markov process, in agreement with exact computations from the Clifford commutant. Finally, the quantization of the rank leaves two hallmarks that distinguish Clifford dynamics from generic monitored circuits: the entropy fluctuations saturate at short scaled times $x\to0$ to an $O(1)$ variance, instead of vanishing, and observables develop a temporal modulation periodic in $\log_q x$, which cannot be captured by the replica approach.

AI.tldr: Monitored Clifford circuits on prime-dimensional qudits purify via a Markovian death process of density-matrix rank, yielding exact scaling functions for Rényi entropies and revealing unique features like O(1) entropy variance and log-periodic modulation absent in generic monitored circuits.
AI.motivation: Purification dynamics in monitored quantum circuits requires the replica trick with delicate analytic continuation. The authors seek a simpler, exact description for Clifford circuits that bypasses this complexity.
AI.method: The authors show that monitored Clifford circuits on L qudits of prime dimension q reduce, in the scaling limit, to a Markovian death process of the density-matrix rank descending from infinity. They compute full scaling functions for all Rényi entropies, perform exact stabilizer simulations at q=2,3,5, and analyze the replica problem as a tilted version of the same Markov process via the Clifford commutant.
AI.result: All Rényi entropies collapse onto a universal curve ⟨S(x)⟩ confirmed by simulations. The replica problem maps to a tilted Markov process matching exact commutant computations. Two distinctive hallmarks of Clifford dynamics emerge: entropy fluctuations saturate to O(1) variance at short scaled times (instead of vanishing), and observables exhibit temporal modulation periodic in log_q x.
AI.conclusion: Monitored Clifford circuits admit an exact, replica-free description of purification dynamics, with unique features (O(1) variance, log-periodic modulation) that distinguish them from generic monitored circuits and cannot be captured by the replica approach.

title: Feynman's clock and hierarchy-informed sampling for quantum error mitigation
summary: Near-term physical implementations of quantum algorithms require efficient quantum error mitigation schemes to reduce quantum noise. In this letter we propose a new mitigation technique, by extending the applicability of our BBGKY-ISM scheme from quantum simulations of spin chains to arbitrary quantum circuits. We map executions of quantum circuits using Feynman's clock Hamiltonian to the Hamiltonian dynamics of a corresponding quantum system, whose time evolution obeys a BBGKY-like hierarchy of equations informing the BBGKY-ISM mitigation. We show that the method's classical and quantum overheads are polynomial in the circuit size and in the number of qubits. We apply our method to numerical simulations of tunable Bell state preparation circuits under state-of-the-art quantum noise, and numerically demonstrate its systematic and controllable quantum error reduction capability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a BBGKY-ISM quantum error mitigation scheme that maps quantum circuits to Hamiltonian dynamics via Feynman's clock Hamiltonian, achieving polynomial overhead in circuit size and qubit count, with demonstrated error reduction in simulated Bell state preparation circuits under realistic noise.
AI.motivation: Near-term quantum computing requires efficient error mitigation schemes to reduce quantum noise in practical implementations.
AI.method: Extends the BBGKY-ISM scheme from spin chain simulations to arbitrary quantum circuits by mapping circuit executions to Hamiltonian dynamics using Feynman's clock Hamiltonian, where time evolution follows a BBGKY-like hierarchy of equations.
AI.result: The classical and quantum overheads are polynomial in circuit size and number of qubits. Numerical simulations of tunable Bell state preparation circuits under state-of-the-art quantum noise demonstrate systematic and controllable quantum error reduction.
AI.conclusion: BBGKY-ISM is a viable polynomial-overhead error mitigation technique for arbitrary quantum circuits, with demonstrated effectiveness under realistic noise conditions.

title: Secret Key Rate Analysis of Distribution Matching Algorithms for Discrete-Modulated CV-QKD
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures. Under consideration for publication in the IEEE Transactions on Communications
summary: Continuous variable quantum key distribution protocols (CV-QKD) with discrete modulation have been intensively investigated to bridge the gap between ideal Gaussian modulation and modern coherent optical communication systems. To mitigate the penalty of discrete modulation, probabilistic constellation shaping (PCS) is applied to the modulation format and is typically performed by distribution matching (DM) algorithms. In this paper, we address the application of DM algorithms to perform PCS in CV-QKD protocols. We investigate the impact of approximating optimized Maxwell-Boltzman distributions with DM algorithms based on Huffman (HDM) and constant composition (CCDM) codes on the protocol's secret key rate (SKR) and tolerance to excess noise. Our results show that specifically symbol-by-symbol HDM degrades the SKR by at least 30\%, whereas CCDM matches the optimal SKR with code length of $10^3$ or more symbols. Furthermore, we also provide a statistical analysis of symbol dependence for both approaches, showing that CCDM must operate with blocks of at least $10^5$ symbols for the correlations become negligible. Finally, we propose an algorithm to generate independent symbols following near-optimal distributions.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how distribution matching (DM) algorithms—specifically Huffman (HDM) and constant composition (CCDM) coding—affect the performance of probabilistic constellation shaping (PCS) in CV-QKD with discrete modulation, finding that CCDM approaches optimal secret key rates with sufficient block length while HDM degrades SKR by at least 30%, and proposes an algorithm for near-optimal independent symbol generation.
AI.motivation: To bridge the performance gap between ideal Gaussian modulation and practical discrete modulation in CV-QKD by applying probabilistic constellation shaping via distribution matching algorithms, while assessing the actual impact of these algorithms on key rate and noise tolerance.
AI.method: The paper applies Huffman distribution matching (HDM) and constant composition distribution matching (CCDM) to approximate optimized Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions in CV-QKD, analyzing their effect on secret key rate and excess noise tolerance, along with statistical analysis of symbol dependence, and proposes a new algorithm for generating near-optimal independent symbols.
AI.result: HDM degrades SKR by at least 30% due to symbol-by-symbol operation; CCDM matches optimal SKR with code length ≥ 10³ symbols; CCDM requires blocks of ≥ 10⁵ symbols for symbol correlations to become negligible.
AI.conclusion: CCDM is a viable DM approach for PCS in CV-QKD given sufficient block length, while HDM introduces significant penalty; the proposed algorithm enables generation of near-optimal independent symbols.

title: Entanglement-assisted remote energy transfer
summary: Currently, remote energy transfer and immunity to dissipation are hot topics in quantum batteries (QBs). In this work, we propose a protocol to realize energy transfer between two remote atoms (a quantum charger and a quantum battery) each coupled to a separate optical cavity with the cavities connected by a fiber. The cavities and fiber are coupled to their individual baths. After optimizing inter-system couplings to achieve an efficient transfer, we uncover the effect of suppressing dissipation by introducing parity deformation of the cavities fields. We also prove that the charger-battery entanglement is a consumable resource for energy storage: it is initially stored until the charger and battery reach energy balance, and then subsequently consumed to maintain the increase in energy stored in the battery. The present scheme is the first execution of energy transfer to a distant battery assisted by entanglement, which may help better understand quantum thermodynamics and open new possibilities toward harnessing decoherence as a resource to improve the charging performance of QBs.

AI.tldr: Proposes a protocol for remote energy transfer between two atoms (quantum charger and battery) via optical cavities connected by fiber, using parity deformation to suppress dissipation and demonstrating that charger-battery entanglement is a consumable resource for energy storage.
AI.motivation: To address the challenges of remote energy transfer and dissipation immunity in quantum batteries, and to understand the role of entanglement in energy storage processes.
AI.method: A setup with two atoms each coupled to separate optical cavities connected by a fiber, where cavities and fiber are coupled to individual baths. Inter-system couplings are optimized, and parity deformation of cavity fields is introduced to suppress dissipation.
AI.result: Optimized coupling enables efficient energy transfer; parity deformation suppresses dissipation; charger-battery entanglement acts as a consumable resource — stored initially until energy balance is reached, then consumed to maintain the battery's energy increase.
AI.conclusion: This is the first demonstration of entanglement-assisted energy transfer to a distant quantum battery, offering insights into quantum thermodynamics and suggesting decoherence can be harnessed as a resource to improve QB charging performance.

title: Universal spin-squeezing dynamics in spinor condensates
summary: The production of large-scale entangled states is one of the main goals of next-generation quantum technologies, with an immediate potential for applications in the context of entanglement-assisted quantum sensing. A very promising platform to achieve this goal is offered by ultracold spinor gases, made of atoms with a large internal spin sensitive to magnetic fields. Here we show that the native spin-changing collisions in a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate, combined with an arbitrary quadratic Zeeman shift, can generate scalable spin squeezing in the collective spin of the ensemble, following the universal paradigm of the celebrated one-axis-twisting model. Squeezing dynamics is driven by the quadratic Zeeman shift when this shift is small; and by the spin-changing collisions for large shifts, in the form of stroboscopic squeezing. Turning off the Zeeman shift freezes out the collective-spin dynamics, so that the ensuing collective spin dynamics can be uniquely governed by an external field to be sensed. Our theoretical results pave the way for the use of spinor Bose gases with a large spin in fundamental studies of entanglement, as well as in advanced metrological applications.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that spin-changing collisions in a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate, combined with a tunable quadratic Zeeman shift, can generate scalable spin squeezing following the one-axis-twisting model, enabling entanglement-enhanced quantum sensing.
AI.motivation: The production of large-scale entangled states is a key goal for next-generation quantum technologies, particularly for entanglement-assisted quantum sensing. Ultracold spinor gases with large internal spin offer a promising platform for this purpose.
AI.method: The authors show that native spin-changing collisions in a spinor Bose-Einstein condensate, combined with an arbitrary quadratic Zeeman shift, can generate scalable spin squeezing via the one-axis-twisting paradigm. The squeezing dynamics is driven by the quadratic Zeeman shift when small, and by spin-changing collisions (stroboscopic squeezing) for large shifts. Turning off the Zeeman shift freezes collective-spin dynamics, allowing the spin to be governed solely by an external field.
AI.result: The system can generate scalable spin squeezing in the collective spin of the ensemble, following the universal one-axis-twisting model, with tunable control over the squeezing mechanism via the quadratic Zeeman shift.
AI.conclusion: These results pave the way for using large-spin spinor Bose gases in fundamental entanglement studies and advanced metrological applications.

title: How thermal is a filtered state?
summary: Quantum many-body states with sufficiently low energy variance can serve as approximations to thermal states, and they may be prepared by energy filtering simple pure states. In this work, we examine how narrow the filter width must be to guarantee thermal behavior. To this end, we analyze the problem in the Floquet regime, where filtered states are found to be equivalent to time averages. This equivalence allows us to reproduce the distinct Rényi-$α$ entropy scalings as reported in [Morettini et al., Physical Review Letters 133, 240401 (2024)]. Crucially, we show that under the Floquet eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, the trace distance between Floquet-filtered states and thermal states is bounded by the square root of filter width. We further demonstrate that these results extend naturally to the conventional Hamiltonian setting by mapping Hamiltonian-filtered states to their Floquet counterparts.

AI.tldr: This paper examines how narrow the energy filter width must be for filtered quantum many-body states to approximate thermal states, showing in the Floquet regime that the trace distance between filtered and thermal states scales as the square root of the filter width under the Floquet eigenstate thermalization hypothesis.
AI.motivation: To determine the minimum energy filter width required for filtered pure states to reliably approximate thermal states, and to establish rigorous bounds on their distinguishability.
AI.method: The authors analyze energy filtering in the Floquet regime, establishing an equivalence between filtered states and time averages. They then derive bounds on the trace distance between Floquet-filtered states and thermal states using the Floquet eigenstate thermalization hypothesis, and extend these results to conventional Hamiltonian systems through a mapping technique.
AI.result: The trace distance between Floquet-filtered states and thermal states is bounded by the square root of the filter width. The work also reproduces distinct Rényi-α entropy scalings reported in prior literature, and shows that Hamiltonian results follow naturally from the Floquet analysis via mapping.
AI.conclusion: A square-root scaling relation governs the trade-off between filter width and thermal approximation accuracy, providing a quantitative criterion for preparing thermal states via energy filtering. The Floquet formalism offers a unifying framework for analyzing both Floquet and Hamiltonian filtered states.

title: A "squeezed polaron" variational wavefunction for the spin boson model
summary: The localization transition of the sub-Ohmic spin-boson model generates boson bath correlations that are, at low frequencies, analytically inaccessible to standard coherent-state-polaron variational ansatzes. In this paper, we introduce a ``squeezed polaron'' wavefunction incorporating generic Gaussian boson-boson correlations induced by the spin impurity. This gives the correct critical power-law scaling of bath observables near the localization transition together with a systematically improved ground state energy and a more accurate determination of the critical coupling. Our wavefunction captures the correct mean-field nature of the transition in the deep sub-Ohmic region. It also displays non-mean-field critical exponents in the shallow sub-Ohmic regime. Using the squeezed polaron as a starting point, we derive scattering phase shifts for bosons, and show how they encode the emergent energy scale that vanishes at the localization transition.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a "squeezed polaron" wavefunction to study the sub-Ohmic spin-boson model's localization transition, capturing Gaussian boson-boson correlations that standard methods miss. This improves ground state energy, critical coupling accuracy, and correctly predicts both mean-field and non-mean-field critical exponents depending on the sub-Ohmic regime, while also deriving scattering phase shifts that encode the vanishing energy scale at the transition.
AI.motivation: Standard coherent-state-polaron variational ansatzes cannot analytically access low-frequency boson bath correlations near the localization transition of the sub-Ohmic spin-boson model.
AI.method: The authors introduce a "squeezed polaron" wavefunction that incorporates generic Gaussian boson-boson correlations induced by the spin impurity, and derive scattering phase shifts for bosons from this starting point.
AI.result: The squeezed polaron yields correct critical power-law scaling of bath observables, improved ground state energy, more accurate critical coupling, correct mean-field nature in the deep sub-Ohmic region, and non-mean-field critical exponents in the shallow sub-Ohmic regime. Scattering phase shifts encode the emergent energy scale vanishing at the transition.
AI.conclusion: The squeezed polaron wavefunction provides a systematically improved variational description of the sub-Ohmic spin-boson localization transition, capturing correlation effects beyond standard polaron methods.

title: Explaining the magnitude of Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity via electron-electron exchange
summary: Chiral molecular structure can couple to electron spin, leading to unexpected spin polarization effects. This Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) was first reported for DNA molecules adsorbed on gold but its microscopic origin remains unclear. We demonstrated though simulation that the exchange arising from electron-electron Coulomb interactions within the self-consistent mean field (Hartree--Fock) approximation can yield significant ($\sim 2\%$) spin polarisation for $3$-methylcyclohexanone adsorbed on Cu(111) amplifying a much smaller ($\sim 0.0014\%$) initial bias, consistent with experiment. Symmetry considerations ensure the result is physically meaningful, while its ab-initio nature ensures all parameters are physically realistic. This amplification is connected to existing studies on spin-symmetry breaking in Hartree--Fock, providing a new pathway for understanding the magnitude of CISS as an emergent phenomenon of interacting electrons.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates via ab-initio simulation that electron-electron Coulomb exchange within the Hartree-Fock approximation can amplify a tiny initial spin bias (~0.0014%) to a significant ~2% spin polarization for 3-methylcyclohexanone on Cu(111), offering a new mechanism for understanding the Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) effect.
AI.motivation: The microscopic origin of the Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) effect, first observed for DNA on gold, remains unclear despite experimental reports. This work aims to elucidate the physical mechanism underlying CISS.
AI.method: Self-consistent mean-field (Hartree-Fock) approximation simulations incorporating electron-electron Coulomb exchange interactions, applied to 3-methylcyclohexanone adsorbed on Cu(111).
AI.result: A small initial spin bias (~0.0014%) is amplified to a significant ~2% spin polarization via exchange interactions, consistent with experimental observations. Symmetry considerations confirm the physical validity of the result.
AI.conclusion: The CISS effect can be understood as an emergent phenomenon of interacting electrons, where Coulomb exchange amplifies spin polarization. This connects to existing studies on spin-symmetry breaking in Hartree-Fock theory.

title: XOR Games at Full Tilt: The Hardness of Binary Nonlocal Games
summary:
It is well known that the quantum value of an XOR nonlocal game, where the winning condition depends only on the XOR of the two players' output bits, may be approximated in polynomial time. We study a variant of the XOR game model, which we call tilted XOR games, where the winning condition can additionally depend on only one of the output bits. We show that this dramatically increases the expressive power: the computational complexity of the problem of approximating the quantum value of tilted XOR games to constant precision is RE-complete. Also, our result extends to succinct versions of tilted XOR games, where the questions can be polynomial-length binary strings, generated by a polynomial-time verifier.
  For classical strategies, the distinction between XOR games and tilted XOR games is inconsequential. Håstad (J. ACM, 2001) shows that they are both NP-complete to approximate, by using a reduction from linear systems to XOR games. Our approach is to show that this is also quantum-sound, but as a reduction from linear system games to tilted XOR games.
  Since titled XOR games are a special case of binary games (where each party outputs a single bit), our result implies that binary games are RE-hard to approximate.

AI.tldr: The paper studies tilted XOR games, a variant of XOR nonlocal games where the winning condition can depend on XOR of outputs and individual output bits. While XOR games are approximable in polynomial time quantumly, tilted XOR games are RE-complete to approximate to constant precision. This shows binary games are RE-hard to approximate.
AI.motivation: To understand how adding dependence on individual output bits (rather than just XOR) changes the computational complexity of approximating quantum values of nonlocal games, particularly showing a dramatic jump from polynomial-time to RE-complete.
AI.method: The paper reduces the quantum value approximation of linear system games to tilted XOR games, showing the reduction is quantum-sound. This leverages the known RE-completeness of linear system games.
AI.result: Approximating the quantum value of tilted XOR games to constant precision is RE-complete. Since tilted XOR games are a special case of binary games, binary games are also RE-hard to approximate.
AI.conclusion: The expressive power of XOR games increases dramatically when the winning condition can depend on individual output bits in addition to their XOR. This establishes a sharp complexity-theoretic boundary between tractable and undecidable quantum value approximation.

title: Correlation Localization in Waveguide QED with Delayed Interactions
summary: We study the atom-atom correlation length in an atomic array coupled to a waveguide under the Bragg condition with delayed non-Markovian interactions caused by a finite photon propagation time. Starting from a single excited atom, the excitation partially spreads among all atoms, reaching a steady state. The remaining excitation localizes near the initially excited atom, and the atom-atom correlation length decreases as a power law with the interaction delay. This localization phenomenon reveals how the delay-induced non-Markovian behavior affects the correlation transport in waveguide QED systems.

AI.tldr: Study of atom-atom correlation length in waveguide-coupled atomic arrays under Bragg condition with delayed non-Markovian interactions, showing power-law localization of excitation near the initially excited atom as interaction delay increases.
AI.motivation: To understand how finite photon propagation time (non-Markovian delay) affects correlation transport and localization in waveguide QED systems under Bragg conditions.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of an atomic array coupled to a waveguide under Bragg condition, incorporating delayed non-Markovian interactions due to finite photon propagation time. Starting from a single excited atom, the system evolution is studied to examine the steady-state excitation distribution and atom-atom correlation length.
AI.result: The excitation partially spreads among all atoms and reaches a steady state, with remaining excitation localized near the initially excited atom. The atom-atom correlation length decreases as a power law with increasing interaction delay.
AI.conclusion: Delay-induced non-Markovian behavior is shown to be a key factor controlling correlation transport and localization in waveguide QED systems, with the correlation length exhibiting power-law dependence on interaction delay.

title: Enhanced two-photon sources in a cavity-coupled two-atom system
summary: We propose a component-selective scheme for improving two-photon sources in a cavity-coupled two-atom system, where a single cavity mode interacts with two two-level atoms driven by phase-controlled classical fields of the same frequency. By controlling the atomic detunings and driving phase, the system can be tailored toward optimized cavity-field two-photon blockade or strongly correlated fluorescence photon-pair emission. When the two-cavity-photon component is enhanced, the cavity field exhibits optimized two-photon blockade with simultaneous suppression of unwanted one- and three-photon components at a comparable two-photon population. In another parameter regime, strongly correlated fluorescence photon pairs can also be generated from the two atoms by selecting the double-atomic-excitation component in the same two-excitation manifold. This approach provides a route toward high-quality and versatile two-photon sources, with potential applications in few-photon quantum optics and quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: A scheme using a cavity-coupled two-atom system with phase-controlled driving fields enables selective enhancement of two-photon components, achieving optimized two-photon blockade or correlated fluorescence photon-pair emission for high-quality two-photon sources.
AI.motivation: To develop a high-quality, versatile two-photon source by selectively enhancing the two-photon component while suppressing unwanted one- and three-photon components in a cavity-coupled two-atom system.
AI.method: A cavity mode interacts with two two-level atoms driven by phase-controlled classical fields of the same frequency; the system is controlled via atomic detunings and driving phase to tailor the cavity-field two-photon blockade or fluorescence photon-pair emission.
AI.result: Optimized two-photon blockade with simultaneous suppression of one- and three-photon components at comparable two-photon population; strongly correlated fluorescence photon pairs generated via double-atomic-excitation component selection.
AI.conclusion: This approach provides a route toward high-quality and versatile two-photon sources for few-photon quantum optics and quantum information processing.

title: Anyon-induced non-Hermitian topological phases
summary: We show that anyonic exchange statistics can activate non-Hermitian point-gap topology in models that are topologically trivial in its absence. The emergent topology oscillates more rapidly with the statistical phase as the anyon number increases, and exhibits a parity dependence on the particle number. A perturbative analysis reveals the mechanism: fractional statistics induces a mismatch between momentum terms that, combined with sublattice-dependent dissipation, produces particle-number-dependent non-reciprocity and complex spectral winding. As these effects rely on the formation and exchange of interaction-bound anyons, our results establish exchange statistics as a resource for enabling non-Hermitian topology under programmed dissipation.

AI.tldr: Anyonic exchange statistics can activate non-Hermitian point-gap topology in topologically trivial models, with the topology oscillating with statistical phase, showing parity-dependent particle number effects, and establishing exchange statistics as a resource for non-Hermitian topology under programmed dissipation.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that anyonic exchange statistics can serve as a resource to activate non-Hermitian point-gap topology in models that are topologically trivial in the absence of such statistics.
AI.method: Perturbative analysis revealing that fractional statistics induces a momentum term mismatch which, combined with sublattice-dependent dissipation, produces particle-number-dependent non-reciprocity and complex spectral winding.
AI.result: Exchange statistics activate non-Hermitian topology, with oscillations that become more rapid as anyon number increases and exhibit parity dependence on particle number.
AI.conclusion: Exchange statistics are a resource for enabling non-Hermitian topology under programmed dissipation, relying on the formation and exchange of interaction-bound anyons.

title: A quantum model for synchronizing finite state transition systems
summary: We propose a quantum model for finding a resetting input sequence (RS) which can take a finite state transition system (FA), to particular state independent of its current state. The complexity of finding such sequences for various types of FA can be NP-Hard or even PSPACE-Complete. To this end, we represent the FA states, inputs, and transition function in quantum space. Accordingly, we propose a model to represent the execution of an input sequence of a particular length $l$ starting form an initial FA state. The model is extended considering the application in superposition of all input sequences of length $l$ to an initial state of the FA. The model is further extended considering the application of all input sequences to all initial states of the FA capturing for every input sequence the collection (ordered list) of states reached by applying the sequence to all states of the FA. The amplitude amplification algorithm is then used as it combines similar collections of reached states while preserving all input sequences that reach these collections. A Grover search for a reached collection where its elements correspond to the same FA state provides a RS for the FA. Our approach offers a quadratic gain over the exponential complexity of traditional brute-force method, which is the only method that can be applied to a general FA class. As a proof of concept we provide results of several simulated FAs on a quantum simulator.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum algorithm to find resetting input sequences (RS) for finite state transition systems (FA) by representing FA states, inputs, and transitions in quantum space, using superposition of all input sequences, and applying amplitude amplification (Grover's search) to achieve a quadratic speedup over classical brute-force methods, with proof-of-concept simulations on a quantum simulator.
AI.motivation: Finding resetting sequences (RS) for finite automata is computationally hard (NP-Hard to PSPACE-Complete), and no efficient classical algorithm exists for general FA classes. The only universal method is brute-force, which is exponentially expensive, motivating the need for a quantum approach to achieve computational advantage.
AI.method: The FA states, inputs, and transition function are represented in quantum space. The model first encodes execution of a single input sequence of length l, then extends to superposition of all input sequences of length l applied to a single initial state, and further to all input sequences applied to all initial states. The collection of reached states (ordered list) for each input sequence is captured. Amplitude amplification (Grover search) is used to combine similar collections and find a collection where all elements converge to the same FA state, indicating a valid resetting sequence.
AI.result: The quantum approach provides a quadratic gain (O(2^(l/2)) in Grover's oracle calls) over the exponential complexity of classical brute-force methods (O(2^l)). Results from simulated FAs on a quantum simulator are provided as proof of concept.
AI.conclusion: A quantum model for finding resetting sequences in finite automata is proposed, achieving quadratic speedup over brute-force methods, demonstrated on simulated FAs.

title: Tomography of a Macroscopic Quantum State influenced by Classical Self-Gravity
summary: Macroscopic optomechanical systems offer a promising testbed for distinguishing whether gravity acts as a quantum interaction or as a classical field. Schrodinger-Newton (SN) theory is the nonrelativistic limit of semi-classical gravity where quantum matter couples to classical gravity. Based on SN theory, this work investigates how classical self-gravity affects continuous quantum state tomography of a macroscopic mechanical oscillator monitored by variable-angle homodyne detection. In the Schrodinger-Newton (SN) theory, the measurement record arises from a different conditional test mass dynamics from that in quantum-gravity (QG)/standard quantum mechanics, consequently, applying the QG-optimised reconstruction map introduces an additional state-dependent contribution. We show that this contribution makes the reconstructed covariance depend on the chosen set of tomography angles and can drive the SN covariance--after QG filtering--outside the standard Gaussian-covariance domain set by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. We quantify the resulting QG-SN distinguishability via the Hellinger distance and analyse its dependence on measurement strength and temperature. We then formulate the same issue in the broader setting of nonlinear quantum mechanics: when the system's conditional dynamics during the readout process depends on the state being inferred, the tomographic map acquires nonlinear, model-dependent corrections to the usual Radon or Gaussian reconstruction map.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how Schrödinger-Newton (SN) theory—where quantum matter couples to classical gravity—affects continuous quantum state tomography of macroscopic mechanical oscillators. The authors show that applying quantum-gravity-optimized reconstruction to SN measurement data introduces state-dependent errors, causing reconstructed covariances to violate the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. They quantify distinguishability using Hellinger distance and generalize the issue to nonlinear quantum mechanics where conditional dynamics depend on the inferred state.
AI.motivation: Macroscopic optomechanical systems can test whether gravity is quantum or classical. SN theory provides a testable semiclassical gravity model, and the authors aim to determine how classical self-gravity corrupts quantum state tomography when using reconstruction maps optimized for quantum gravity/standard quantum mechanics.
AI.method: The authors model a macroscopic mechanical oscillator monitored by variable-angle homodyne detection under SN dynamics. They compare the measurement record from SN conditional dynamics to that from quantum gravity, apply the QG-optimized Gaussian reconstruction map to SN data, compute the resulting covariance matrix, and quantify the discrepancy via the Hellinger distance as a function of measurement strength and temperature.
AI.result: Applying QG-optimized tomography to SN dynamics introduces an additional state-dependent contribution that makes the reconstructed covariance depend on the chosen tomography angles. This can drive the covariance outside the standard Gaussian domain set by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.
AI.conclusion: The QG-SN distinguishability is measurable via Hellinger distance and depends on measurement strength and temperature. The broader implication is that anytime conditional dynamics depend on the inferred state (as in nonlinear quantum mechanics), tomographic reconstruction acquires nonlinear, model-dependent corrections beyond standard Radon/Gaussian maps.

title: Operator-frame geometry of non-compact quantum systems with frame-vacuum phase transitions
summary: We formulate the geometric structure of non-compact bosonic quantum systems in regimes where vacuum instability renders the relevant quantum states non-normalizable, causing conventional state-space quantum geometry -- described by the Berry connection, curvature, and quantum metric -- to become ill-defined. To overcome this breakdown, we develop a formulation of quantum geometry at the level of canonical operator frames, allowing for complexified Bogoliubov-Valatin transformations that lift the requirement that creation operators be Hermitian conjugates of annihilation operators. Canonical operator frames are defined as choices of bosonic creation and annihilation operators realizing the canonical commutation relations. A natural equivalence relation among such frames generalizes the phase ambiguity of quantum states and determines a parameter space that analytically extends the stable-regime parameter space. The space of canonical operator frames forms a principal bundle over parameter space -- the operator-frame bundle -- equipped with a natural Ehresmann connection that defines parallel transport while preserving the canonical commutation relations. In the stable regime, this construction reduces to the Berry connection, while more generally it yields a well-defined operator-space quantum geometric tensor (QGT) that remains valid across vacuum instabilities. Using the framework of rigged Hilbert spaces, we define a notion of quantum frame vacuum and obtain a consistent state-space QGT. Focusing on a single bosonic mode, we demonstrate analyticity of the QGT across the quantum frame-vacuum phase transition and present the corresponding phase diagram on the complexified squeezing-parameter plane. We further introduce a realistic physical setting that allows continuous paths connecting stable and unstable regimes, along which the QGT evolves smoothly across Stokes lines.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a framework for quantum geometry in non-compact bosonic systems where vacuum instability causes standard geometric tools (Berry connection, quantum metric) to break down. By introducing canonical operator frames and complexified Bogoliubov-Valatin transformations, the authors define an operator-frame bundle with an Ehresmann connection that generalizes the Berry connection to unstable regimes. They demonstrate analyticity of the quantum geometric tensor across vacuum instabilities and illustrate the formalism on a single bosonic mode.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum geometry (Berry connection, quantum metric) fails in non-compact bosonic systems when vacuum instability leads to non-normalizable quantum states. The authors aim to extend geometric tools to such regimes where the standard state-space approach becomes ill-defined.
AI.method: The authors formulate quantum geometry at the level of canonical operator frames, using complexified Bogoliubov-Valatin transformations that relax the Hermitian-conjugate relation between creation and annihilation operators. They construct an operator-frame bundle with a natural Ehresmann connection and employ rigged Hilbert spaces to define a quantum frame vacuum and a consistent state-space quantum geometric tensor.
AI.result: The operator-frame bundle with its Ehresmann connection reduces to the Berry connection in the stable regime and remains well-defined across vacuum instabilities. For a single bosonic mode, the quantum geometric tensor is shown to be analytic across the quantum frame-vacuum phase transition, with a phase diagram on the complexified squeezing-parameter plane. The QGT evolves smoothly across Stokes lines along continuous paths connecting stable and unstable regimes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed operator-frame formalism provides a consistent generalization of quantum geometry that remains valid across vacuum instabilities, enabling the study of geometric properties in regimes previously inaccessible due to non-normalizable states.

title: Bayesian Gill-Massar Bound: An Attainable Lower Bound for Qubit Parameter Estimation
summary: We study lower bounds for Bayesian quantum parameter estimation, with a particular focus on qubit models. While several lower bounds on the Bayes risk have been proposed, including the Bayesian symmetric logarithmic derivative (B-SLD) type bound and the Bayesian Nagaoka-Hayashi (B-NH) bound, there is no definite proof available to show they are attainable except for special cases. Thus, identifying attainable bounds together with their corresponding optimal measurement strategies remains a central open problem in Bayesian quantum estimation. In this work, we introduce a new Bayesian lower bound, referred to as the Bayesian Gill-Massar (B-GM) bound, inspired by the logic of Gill-Massar bound in point estimation. We derive an analytical closed-form expression of the bound and show that it is attainable for any qubit model. In particular, we prove that the optimal Bayesian strategy can be realized by a projection-valued measure associated with a single effective direction determined by the weight matrix and the B-SLD-type Fisher information matrix. We provide numerical comparisons between the B-GM, B-NH, and B-SLD-type bounds in higher-dimensional models. Our results show that the B-GM bound has a limitation in high-dimensional models with few parameters, since it can be negative.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Bayesian Gill-Massar (B-GM) bound for quantum parameter estimation, provides a closed-form expression, proves attainability for qubit models, identifies the optimal measurement strategy, and compares bounds numerically in higher dimensions.
AI.motivation: Existing Bayesian lower bounds (B-SLD, B-NH) lack general attainability proofs and optimal measurement strategies. Identifying attainable bounds with corresponding optimal measurements is a central open problem in Bayesian quantum estimation.
AI.method: The authors propose the B-GM bound inspired by the Gill-Massar bound from point estimation. They derive an analytical closed-form expression, prove attainability via projection-valued measurements along a single effective direction determined by the weight matrix and B-SLD-type Fisher information, and perform numerical comparisons in higher-dimensional models.
AI.result: The B-GM bound is attainable for any qubit model. The optimal Bayesian strategy is realized by a PVM along a single effective direction. In higher-dimensional models with few parameters, the B-GM bound can be negative, revealing a limitation.
AI.conclusion: The B-GM bound provides a new, provably attainable lower bound for qubit Bayesian estimation, but has limitations in high-dimensional sparse-parameter settings due to potential negativity.

title: Quantum Recurrence Plot Algorithm Based on Quantum Principal Component Analysis
summary: Recurrence Plot (RP) is a method employed to analyze the periodicity, chaoticity, and nonlinear characteristics of complex systems. Quantum Principal Component Analysis (QPCA), on the other hand, achieves dimensionality reduction of sample data using density matrices based on quantum circuits. We improve the distance threshold function of the recurrence plot algorithm using a density operator conceptually equivalent to the covariance matrix, integrate it with quantum circuits, and thereby develop a Quantum Recurrence Plot (QRP) algorithm. This algorithm achieves ultra-high efficiency in parallel computing, reduces computational costs, and simultaneously upgrades the traditional grayscale recurrence plot to colored heatmaps, enabling a better revelation of the system's dynamical characteristics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Quantum Recurrence Plot (QRP) algorithm that integrates quantum computing with recurrence plots by replacing the distance threshold function with a density operator, enabling ultra-efficient parallel computation, reduced costs, and colored heatmap visualization for improved analysis of dynamical system characteristics.
AI.motivation: To improve the efficiency and expressiveness of traditional Recurrence Plots by leveraging quantum computing principles, specifically Quantum Principal Component Analysis (QPCA) and density operators, to achieve parallel computing gains and better visualization of system dynamics.
AI.method: The distance threshold function in the recurrence plot algorithm is improved by using a density operator (conceptually equivalent to the covariance matrix), which is then integrated with quantum circuits to form the Quantum Recurrence Plot (QRP) algorithm.
AI.result: The QRP algorithm achieves ultra-high efficiency in parallel computing, reduces computational costs, and upgrades traditional grayscale recurrence plots to colored heatmaps that better reveal system dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Quantum Recurrence Plots offer a more efficient and visually informative approach to analyzing periodicity, chaoticity, and nonlinear characteristics of complex systems compared to traditional recurrence plots.

title: Spectral Chaos Does Not Determine Quantum Mpemba Crossings
summary: In a symmetry-restoration quantum Mpemba effect, an initial state with stronger local symmetry breaking can lose that memory faster than a state that starts closer to the symmetric manifold. We test whether this local ordering reversal is organized by chaotic thermalization in a clean U(1)-conserving spin chain, comparing spectral level statistics with crossings of the entanglement asymmetry for the same Hamiltonians. We find that Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE)-like level statistics alone do not determine whether Mpemba crossings occur. Across field textures, GOE-like spectra can occur with or without entanglement-asymmetry crossings, and crossings can also appear away from the GOE reference. A near-staggered detuned control further shows that even an inversion of the total charge-sector coherence need not produce an entanglement-asymmetry crossing. Thus the crossing response is controlled not by spectral chaos alone, but by how local charge-sector coherence enters the reduced density matrix.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether the quantum Mpemba effect (local symmetry restoration reversal) in a U(1)-conserving spin chain is organized by chaotic thermalization. Using spectral level statistics and entanglement asymmetry, they find that GOE-like spectra alone do not predict Mpemba crossings; crossings can occur with or without GOE statistics, and vice versa. The crossing is governed by how local charge-sector coherence enters the reduced density matrix, not by spectral chaos alone.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the symmetry-restoration quantum Mpemba effect (where a more strongly symmetry-broken initial state restores symmetry faster) is governed by chaotic thermalization, as characterized by spectral level statistics (GOE).
AI.method: Comparing spectral level statistics (GOE reference) with entanglement asymmetry crossings in a clean U(1)-conserving spin chain across various field textures. Also tests a near-staggered detuned control to examine the role of total charge-sector coherence.
AI.result: GOE-like level statistics do not determine Mpemba crossings: GOE spectra can appear with or without crossings, and crossings can occur away from GOE reference. Additionally, inverting total charge-sector coherence does not necessarily produce an entanglement-asymmetry crossing.
AI.conclusion: The quantum Mpemba crossing is not controlled by spectral chaos alone, but by how local charge-sector coherence enters the reduced density matrix.

title: Phase-Selected Efficient Single-Photon Frequency Conversion via Local Fano Resonance in a Two-Giant-Atom Waveguide-QED System
summary: Efficient single-photon frequency conversion is investigated in a two-giant-atom waveguide-QED system, where a two-level giant atom and a $Λ$-type three-level giant atom couple to a common one-dimensional waveguide. While the $Λ$-type atom provides the inelastic channel, the two-level atom induces secondary coherent coupling, creating multi-path interference for the converted photon. Using the real-space approach and within the Markovian approximation, we derive analytical four-channel scattering amplitudes and reveal that the inelastic transmission spectrum, governed by three complex resonance poles, exhibits a multi-peak interference pattern. By introducing a local single-pole approximation, we reduce this complex spectrum to a local Fano lineshape, decomposing it into a coherent superposition of a local background term and a single-pole resonant term. The interplay between these two terms-controlled by the photon propagation phase between the giant atoms' coupling points-determines the conversion efficiency, with the background suppression condition leading to a Lorentzian reduction. Based on the single-pole resonance weight, we formulate a phase-selection criterion for highly efficient conversion. Compared with both the small-atom and single $Λ$-type giant-atom models, the two-giant-atom scheme achieves substantially enhanced inelastic transmission over a broader frequency-conversion range. This work reveals how phase-controlled local Fano resonance enables high-efficiency frequency conversion, establishing a general paradigm for engineering resonant light-matter interactions in structured quantum systems.

AI.motivation: To achieve efficient single-photon frequency conversion by exploiting multi-path interference and phase-controlled Fano resonance in a two-giant-atom waveguide-QED system, surpassing the limitations of small-atom and single Λ-type giant-atom models.
AI.method: The authors employ a real-space approach under the Markovian approximation to derive analytical four-channel scattering amplitudes. They introduce a local single-pole approximation to reduce the multi-peak inelastic transmission spectrum to a local Fano lineshape, decomposing it into a coherent superposition of a background term and a single-pole resonant term.

The conversion efficiency is controlled by the photon propagation phase between the giant atoms' coupling points. A phase-selection criterion based on single-pole resonance weight is formulated for highly efficient conversion. The two-giant-atom scheme achieves substantially enhanced inelastic transmission over a broader frequency-conversion range compared to small-atom and single Λ-type giant-atom models.

title: Room-temperature inversionless diamond nitrogen-vacancy electronic spin maser
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, supplementary material (10 pages, 7 figures)
summary: We propose a method to create a room-temperature maser operating at approximately 2.9~GHz frequency using an ensemble of negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy electronic spins (NV) in diamond, without requiring population inversion. Our method considers a DC magnetic field of a few milli-Tesla (mT) applied along the perpendicular direction of an ensemble of NV spins aligned along a common axis. This perpendicular magnetic-field creates superposition states of $|m_{\mathrm{s}}=-1\rangle$ and $|m_{\mathrm{s}}=+1\rangle$ of the NV spin's ground state triplet levels and thereby makes it possible to drive all three transitions in the NV spin ground state. We model the system by including optical pumping of the NV spins, near-resonant driving of two transitions, and coupling the third transition to a near-resonant microwave resonator. Numerical estimates using experimentally realizable parameters show that inversionless masing can be achieved inside the microwave resonator using our method. As an application, we show that the output intensity of an inversionless maser ($1.1\times10^{14}$ spins) can be used for magnetic field sensing with a DC sensitivity on the order of a hundred pT/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$. Our study opens a new direction in room-temperature diamond NV maser devices for quantum technological applications without the requirement of a strong bias magnetic field, as in conventional NV diamond masers.

AI.method: A perpendicular DC magnetic field (few mT) is applied to an ensemble of NV spins aligned along a common axis, creating superposition states of |ms=-1⟩ and |ms=+1⟩, allowing all three ground-state transitions to be driven. The system includes optical pumping, near-resonant driving of two transitions, and coupling the third transition to a near-resonant microwave resonator.

AI.conclusion: This study opens a new direction for room-temperature diamond NV maser devices for quantum technological applications without requiring a strong bias magnetic field, unlike conventional NV diamond masers.

title: Dynamical structure factor with a pumping approach on a trapped-ion quantum computer
summary: Dynamical structure factors (DSF) measured with neutron-scattering experiments provide key insights into the structure of materials. Their computation requires both the preparation of an equilibrium state and the implementation of Hamiltonian dynamics. We demonstrate the feasibility of computing DSF on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer, comparing the DSF of 1D Heisenberg model on $20$ sites, and that of the copper sulfate crystal. To that end, we introduce a pumping approach for computing the DSF $S(q,ω)$ on quantum computers that enables targeting specific arbitrary values of frequencies $ω$. This method time-evolves the initial state using a time-dependent Hamiltonian perturbed by a source term oscillating at the target frequency $ω$. When targeting only a few frequency values, this approach provides a significant reduction in shot overhead compared to previous methods.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates computing dynamical structure factors (DSF) on a trapped-ion quantum computer using a novel frequency-pumping method that reduces shot overhead when targeting specific frequency values.
AI.motivation: Dynamical structure factors (DSF) measured via neutron scattering are crucial for understanding material structure, but their computation requires both equilibrium state preparation and Hamiltonian dynamics, which is challenging for classical methods.
AI.method: The authors introduce a pumping approach that computes DSF S(q,ω) by time-evolving an initial state using a time-dependent Hamiltonian perturbed by a source term oscillating at the target frequency ω, enabling targeted computation of specific frequency values.
AI.result: The method was demonstrated on the Quantinuum Reimei trapped-ion quantum computer for the 1D Heisenberg model (20 sites) and copper sulfate crystal, showing feasibility with significant shot overhead reduction when targeting only a few frequency values.
AI.conclusion: The pumping approach for DSF computation on quantum computers offers a more efficient alternative to previous methods when only a limited set of frequency values is needed.

title: Macroscopic position-position entanglement by photon recoil in Rydberg atoms
summary: Entanglement between two spatially separate matter particles can be generated via many means and often resides in the internal states of particles. Here, via Rydberg blockade in two spatially separate neutral atoms, we find that the photon recoil in Rydberg excitation can push one atom microns away provided the other atom exerts a state-dependent Rydberg-mediated blockade. When the atoms are recaptured by optical traps, a position-position entangled state between two spatially separate atoms can emerge. This realizes a Bell state of two atoms, where the entanglement exists in the position of each atom and the distance between the two possible locations of each atom can be in the hundred-micron regime.

AI.tldr: Two neutral atoms become entangled in their spatial positions via Rydberg blockade, where photon recoil pushes one atom microns away depending on the other atom's state, resulting in a Bell state with hundred-micron-scale spatial separation between possible locations.
AI.motivation: To generate entanglement between spatially separated matter particles, specifically utilizing Rydberg blockade to create a position-position entangled state between two neutral atoms, achieving macroscopic spatial superposition.
AI.method: Rydberg blockade in two spatially separated neutral atoms; photon recoil from Rydberg excitation pushes one atom microns away contingent on a state-dependent Rydberg-mediated blockade from the other atom; atoms are subsequently recaptured by optical traps.
AI.result: A position-position entangled state (Bell state) between two spatially separate atoms is realized, with the distance between the two possible locations of each atom reaching the hundred-micron regime.
AI.conclusion: Rydberg blockade combined with photon recoil can generate spatial-mode entanglement between neutral atoms at macroscopic distances, enabling a new form of matter entanglement where entanglement resides in position rather than internal states.

title: Analytical Landscape of Maximal Magic for Two-Qutrit States and Beyond
summary: Achieving a genuine quantum advantage relies on two distinct non-classical resources that restrict efficient classical simulation: entanglement and magic (nonstabilizerness). We investigate the interplay between these resources by characterizing the Pareto frontiers of extreme magic at fixed entanglement for systems of two qutrits ($d=3$) and two ququints ($d=5$). Unlike the case of two qubits, the Schmidt spectrum for two qutrits features two independent entanglement parameters, resulting in two-dimensional Pareto surfaces. For the lower frontier, we recast the minimal magic as a compact function of concurrence and negativity, with a maximal value of $\ln 2$. For the upper frontier, we determine the maximal stabilizer Rényi entropy to be $M_2 = \ln(81/17) \approx 1.561$, which tightens the previous theoretical bound of $\ln 5\approx 1.609$ and improves on earlier numerical estimates. The maximum magic is achieved at eighteen distinct maxima categorized into three families of six permutation-equivalent spectra. We provide analytical expressions for the maximal magic in the neighborhood of each maximum and for the corresponding maximally magical states which turn out to be Weyl-Heisenberg-covariant fiducial states for mutually unbiased bases. Finally, numerical analysis of two ququints ($d=5$) reveals six permutation-inequivalent maxima with a peak magic value of $M_2 = \ln(625/49) \approx 2.546$. Based on these findings, we conjecture that the maximal magic for a bipartite system of two qudits with prime dimension $d$ is given by $\ln [ d^4 / (2d^2 - 1) ]$, which reproduces the previously known value for qubits, as well as the values derived here for qutrits and ququints.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the trade-off between entanglement and magic (nonstabilizerness) in bipartite qudit systems, deriving Pareto frontiers, tighter bounds on maximal magic, and analytical expressions for maximally magical states; it conjectures a general formula for maximal magic in prime-dimensional two-qudit systems.
AI.motivation: To understand how two distinct non-classical resources—entanglement and magic—interact in quantum systems, and to characterize the fundamental limits of magic given fixed entanglement resources, which is crucial for quantum advantage and classical simulability.
AI.method: Analytical and numerical characterization of Pareto frontiers for two qutrits (d=3) and two ququints (d=5), using the stabilizer Rényi entropy as a magic measure and concurrence/negativity as entanglement measures; identification of symmetry-inequivalent maxima and their analytical forms.
AI.result: For two qutrits, the lower frontier (minimal magic) is compactly expressed as a function of concurrence and negativity with max value ln2; the upper frontier yields maximal magic M₂ = ln(81/17) ≈ 1.561, tightening the previous bound ln5 ≈ 1.609. Eighteen distinct maxima fall into three families. For two ququints, six permutation-inequivalent maxima give peak magic M₂ = ln(625/49) ≈ 2.546. A conjectured general formula for prime d: M₂_max = ln[d⁴/(2d²-1)].
AI.conclusion: The interplay between entanglement and magic yields nontrivial Pareto structures beyond qubits; the proposed general formula unifies results across dimensions and suggests a universal scaling of maximal magic in bipartite prime-dimensional qudit systems.

title: Quantum Computing : A New Frontier for Science and Society
comment: A succint pedagogical report on quantum technology. Last update February 2026

Such architecture represents a complex, multi-layered system that integrates quantum and classical components to enable the execution of quantum algorithms. This manuscript is then organized as follows : first we will introduce the quantum processing unit, the lowest layer of a quantum computer. Then we will progress from the lowest to the higher layer of the system architectures : measurement, circuit control, error correction and mitigation system, the quantum compiler and finally the software stack, with particular emphasis on the interactions between these components

title: Non-Abelian Thouless pumping based on the global adiabatic criterion in Rydberg synthetic lattices
summary: We study a quantum implementation of non-Abelian Thouless pumping in Lieb lattices using Rydberg synthetic dimensions. The lattice is encoded in twelve selected microwave-coupled Rydberg levels, forming a three-cell structure with six degenerate zero-energy states. These zero-energy states define the working subspace for cyclic modulation of the microwave couplings, while the remaining bright states provide the dominant leakage channels at finite evolution time. To choose the relative timing of the Gaussian pulses, we introduce a global adiabatic criterion (GAC), which evaluates the mean value and temporal fluctuation of a nonadiabatic factor obtained from a representative $Λ$-type transfer paradigm. With the resulting timing applied to the full twelve-level pumping dynamics, composing two elementary pumping cycles in opposite temporal orders produces distinct projected population maps. It is exactly consistent with noncommuting matrix-valued adiabatic operations in the zero-energy subspace. We numerically simulate the non-Abelian Thouless pumping using the Lindblad master equation with state-dependent Rydberg loss and representative perturbations. The results show that the GAC-selected timing within the same Gaussian pulse family gives higher target-state population than two literature-adapted Gaussian pulse schedules over the simulated parameter ranges. This quantum implementation of non-Abelian Thouless pumping, enabled by the GAC, marks a major milestone in finite-time geometric control and paves the way for transformative applications in holonomic quantum computing with Rydberg synthetic lattices.

AI.tldr: This paper implements non-Abelian Thouless pumping in a synthetic Rydberg Lieb lattice (12 microwave-coupled levels, 6 zero-energy states) using a global adiabatic criterion (GAC) to time Gaussian pulses. The GAC-optimized timing outperforms literature-adapted schedules, demonstrating noncommuting adiabatic operations and robustness against Rydberg loss.
AI.motivation: To realize non-Abelian Thouless pumping in a controllable quantum system and develop a practical adiabatic criterion (GAC) for finite-time geometric control, enabling holonomic quantum computing.
AI.method: A 12-level Rydberg synthetic Lieb lattice with six degenerate zero-energy states is engineered via microwave couplings. A global adiabatic criterion (GAC) based on a Λ-type transfer paradigm is introduced to optimize Gaussian pulse timing. Non-Abelian pumping is simulated using the Lindblad master equation with state-dependent loss.
AI.result: The GAC-selected timing yields higher target-state population than two literature-adapted Gaussian schedules. Two elementary pumping cycles in opposite orders produce distinct projected population maps, confirming noncommuting matrix-valued adiabatic operations.
AI.conclusion: The GAC-enabled implementation marks a milestone in finite-time geometric control and paves the way for holonomic quantum computing with Rydberg synthetic lattices.

title: Quantum Boomerang Effect in Time-Crystalline Structures
comment: Accepted for publication in Phys. Rev. B
summary: The quantum boomerang effect (QBE) is a unique dynamical signature of Anderson localization, characterized by a launched wavepacket that initially drifts but ultimately returns to its initial position due to fundamental quantum interference. In this work, we theoretically establish and quantitatively characterize the QBE in a time-crystalline structure using a periodically driven quantum particle in a one-dimensional potential well. By constructing maximally localized Floquet-Wannier states and introducing temporal disorder, we rigorously map the continuous Floquet dynamics onto a discrete disordered tight-binding lattice. By positioning a detector at a fixed spatial coordinate, we monitor the temporal evolution of the wavepacket, to extract the mean temporal center of mass of the probability density in a time-crystalline structure. This mean temporal center of mass exhibits an initial ballistic expansion, followed by a pronounced U-turn, and ultimately returns to its initial temporal position after long-time evolution. These results confirm the existence of the complete QBE in the time domain. They also demonstrate that non-trivial dynamics can be explored within time-crystalline systems, even though these structures already possess an inherent temporal periodicity.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes and quantitatively characterizes the quantum boomerang effect (QBE) in a time-crystalline structure by mapping a periodically driven quantum particle in a 1D potential well onto a discrete disordered tight-binding lattice. Monitoring the mean temporal center of mass reveals initial ballistic expansion, a U-turn, and return to the initial temporal position, confirming the QBE in the time domain.
AI.motivation: To extend the quantum boomerang effect, previously studied in spatial Anderson localization, into the time domain using time-crystalline structures, and to demonstrate that nontrivial dynamics can emerge in systems with inherent temporal periodicity.
AI.method: Construct maximally localized Floquet-Wannier states, introduce temporal disorder, map continuous Floquet dynamics onto a discrete disordered tight-binding lattice, and monitor the temporal evolution of the wavepacket's mean temporal center of mass via a fixed-position detector.
AI.result: The mean temporal center of mass shows initial ballistic expansion, a pronounced U-turn, and return to the initial temporal position after long-time evolution, confirming the complete QBE in the time domain.
AI.conclusion: The quantum boomerang effect exists in the time domain within time-crystalline systems, demonstrating that nontrivial dynamical phenomena can be explored despite the inherent temporal periodicity of such structures.

title: Lecture notes on classical and quantum non-Markovianity

summary: The study of non-Markovian quantum processes has attracted significant interest in recent decades, giving rise to several competing notions of quantum non-Markovianity. The correspondence between classical concepts (stochastic matrices, Chapman-Kolmogorov equation) and their quantum analogs (dynamical maps, CP-divisibility) is emphasized throughout.
