title: Resource-Efficient Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection for Large-Scale Molecular Diversity Optimization
summary: Large-scale combinatorial optimization remains demanding for classical heuristics, particularly when dense Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) formulations induce large memory footprints, high CPU utilization, and long execution times. While near-term quantum processors cannot yet deliver unconditional quantum advantage, hybrid architectures can provide practical value by reducing the resource burden. This paper presents a resource-efficiency study of Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection (HQNS), a framework that decomposes large dense QUBO instances into bounded-width quantum subproblems via stochastic frontier selection. We evaluate HQNS on the Maximum Diversity Subset Selection Problem (MDSSP), focusing on the trade-off between solution quality retention and resource consumption. Benchmarks up to N=1000 candidates show that HQNS preserves 99.9908% of the mean diversity score of an 11-restart parallel Simulated Annealing baseline, while reducing wall-clock time by 94.91%, peak CPU utilization by 64.68%, and peak memory usage by 88.61%. The QPU execution time remains bounded within a 6-7 second envelope across scales, indicating that the quantum component is decoupled from the global QUBO dimension when the frontier size is fixed. These results suggest that HQNS provides a resource-aware pathway for deploying hybrid quantum optimization in practical large-scale settings, serving as an efficient architecture for incorporating near-term quantum processors into classical optimization pipelines.

AI.tldr: HQNS decomposes large dense QUBO instances into bounded-width quantum subproblems via stochastic frontier selection, preserving 99.99% of solution quality while reducing wall-clock time by 94.91%, CPU utilization by 64.68%, and memory usage by 88.61% on MDSSP benchmarks up to N=1000.
AI.motivation: Large-scale combinatorial optimization with dense QUBO formulations suffers from large memory footprints, high CPU utilization, and long execution times; near-term quantum processors cannot deliver unconditional quantum advantage alone.
AI.method: Hybrid Quantum Neighborhood Selection (HQNS) framework: decomposes large dense QUBO instances into bounded-width quantum subproblems using stochastic frontier selection, evaluated on Maximum Diversity Subset Selection Problem (MDSSP).
AI.result: On benchmarks up to N=1000: preserves 99.9908% of mean diversity score vs. 11-restart parallel Simulated Annealing; reduces wall-clock time by 94.91%, peak CPU utilization by 64.68%, peak memory usage by 88.61%; QPU execution time bounded within 6-7 seconds.
AI.conclusion: HQNS provides a resource-aware pathway for deploying hybrid quantum optimization in large-scale settings, serving as an efficient architecture for incorporating near-term quantum processors into classical optimization pipelines.

title: Quantum simulation of real-world nonlinear dynamics via Koopman method
summary: Nonlinear dynamics is ubiquitous in nature, ranging from chemical pattern formation to ocean circulation, yet its simulation on quantum computers is fundamentally limited by the unitary nature of quantum evolution. We propose the quantum Koopman method, a data-driven framework that embeds nonlinear dynamics into a learned linear representation and implements the resulting evolution using shallow quantum circuits. This method learns Koopman observables from trajectory data, projects the lifted dynamics onto a finite-dimensional subspace, and decomposes the corresponding non-unitary propagator into parallel spectral channels. We utilize the Koopman method on a superconducting processor to simulate three distinct nonlinear systems, comprising reaction-diffusion dynamics, fluid motion on a sphere, and satellite-derived observations of Gulf Stream currents, employing up to 32 parallel circuits of 10 qubits. These quantum simulations capture the dominant multiscale patterns and statistical signatures of the underlying dynamics, and reveal a transition from performance limited by hardware noise in weakly nonlinear systems to performance limited by finite-dimensional Koopman representations as nonlinear scale interactions increase. This transition identifies a practical boundary for quantum-amenable nonlinear dynamics, establishing a hardware-validated route for simulating moderately nonlinear dynamics on near-term quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantum Koopman method that embeds nonlinear dynamics into a learned linear representation using shallow quantum circuits. Demonstrated on a superconducting processor with up to 32 parallel 10-qubit circuits, it simulates reaction-diffusion, fluid motion on a sphere, and Gulf Stream currents, revealing a transition from hardware-noise-limited to Koopman-representation-limited performance as nonlinearity increases.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear dynamics are ubiquitous in nature but fundamentally difficult to simulate on quantum computers due to the unitary nature of quantum evolution. This work aims to overcome this limitation by developing a data-driven framework that can simulate moderately nonlinear systems on near-term quantum hardware.
AI.method: The quantum Koopman method: (1) learns Koopman observables from trajectory data to embed nonlinear dynamics into a linear representation, (2) projects the lifted dynamics onto a finite-dimensional subspace, and (3) decomposes the non-unitary propagator into parallel spectral channels implemented via shallow quantum circuits.
AI.result: Simulations of three nonlinear systems were performed on a superconducting processor using up to 32 parallel circuits of 10 qubits. The method captures dominant multiscale patterns and statistical signatures. A performance transition was observed: from hardware-noise-limited in weakly nonlinear systems to finite-dimensional Koopman-representation-limited as nonlinear scale interactions increase.
AI.conclusion: The study identifies a practical boundary for quantum-amenable nonlinear dynamics and establishes a hardware-validated route for simulating moderately nonlinear dynamics on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Circuit Depth Reduction of One-Ancilla Quantum Differential Equation Solver via Extrapolation
summary: Solving linear differential equations is a fundamental task in scientific computing and an important primitive for quantum computing. A recent one-ancilla quantum differential equation solver provides a hardware-friendly and locality-preserving approach with provable performance guarantees, making it highly suitable for the early fault-tolerant and near-term regimes. Its simple circuit structure comes with a natural trade-off: the maximum single-run circuit depth scales as $O (1/ε)$ in the target accuracy $ε$. In this work, we reduce this depth by combining the solver with classical step-size postprocessing. By running the one-ancilla solver at a logarithmic number of finite time step sizes and using classical post-processing to cancel leading discretization errors, we reduce the maximum single-run circuit depth to $O(\mathrm{polylog}(1/ε))$ without adding quantum ancillae or sacrificing locality. Technically, extending extrapolation ideas beyond Hamiltonian and Lindbladian dynamics requires regularity estimates for observable maps under nonunitary evolution, which we obtain through a holomorphic extension of the adjoint evolution. Numerical experiments on the Hatano-Nelson model (ODE) and the convection-diffusion equation (PDE) demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach.

AI.tldr: This paper reduces the maximum single-run circuit depth of a one-ancilla quantum differential equation solver from O(1/ε) to O(polylog(1/ε)) by combining it with classical step-size postprocessing (Richardson extrapolation), without adding extra ancillae or sacrificing locality.
AI.motivation: Solving linear differential equations is fundamental in scientific and quantum computing. A recent one-ancilla quantum solver offers hardware-friendly, locality-preserving features but suffers from a maximum single-run circuit depth scaling as O(1/ε) in target accuracy ε. Reducing this depth while maintaining simplicity is crucial for early fault-tolerant and near-term quantum devices.
AI.method: The approach combines the one-ancilla solver with classical step-size postprocessing (Richardson extrapolation). It runs the solver at a logarithmic number of finite time step sizes, then uses classical post-processing to cancel leading discretization errors. This requires regularity estimates for observable maps under nonunitary evolution, obtained via a holomorphic extension of the adjoint evolution.
AI.result: The maximum single-run circuit depth is reduced from O(1/ε) to O(polylog(1/ε)) without adding quantum ancillae or sacrificing locality. Numerical experiments on the Hatano-Nelson model (ODE) and the convection-diffusion equation (PDE) demonstrate effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: By extending extrapolation ideas beyond Hamiltonian and Lindbladian dynamics to nonunitary evolution via holomorphic adjoint evolution, the method achieves exponentially shallower circuits, making the solver more practical for early fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Spectral-width limit on non-Hermitian quantum metrology
summary: Engineered loss, gain, and non-reciprocity can sharply amplify a sensor's response, and exceptional points and the skin effect are widely proposed as routes to more precise quantum sensors. Some predict an exponentially large quantum Fisher information, the quantity that sets the best achievable precision, yet whether this amplified response is genuine measurement information has remained unsettled. We prove that it is not. For any open sensor whose parameter is imprinted coherently by a Hamiltonian, with loss, gain, non-reciprocity, and readout held fixed, the quantum Fisher information is capped by a single quantity, the spread between the largest and smallest energy the generator can impart, independent of the non-Hermitian dynamics. Amplification enlarges the response but not the information. The reported exponential gains arise only when that spread is unbounded, and any finite spread, such as a photon-number cutoff, restores the cap. The same limit governs dissipative probe preparation and spectral singularities. For photonic sensors the cap takes an operator form in which the information of any probe, classical or entangled, is set by the photon's dwell time at the perturbation, and it contains the recently derived scattering limits as special cases. Non-Hermiticity thus shapes a sensor's dynamics but does not source its precision, and the generator's spread and the attainable dwell time benchmark future non-Hermitian sensing proposals.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that non-Hermitian phenomena (exceptional points, skin effect, loss, gain, non-reciprocity) do not fundamentally enhance measurement precision in quantum sensing. The quantum Fisher information is fundamentally capped by the energy spread of the generator, regardless of non-Hermitian dynamics. Reported exponential gains require unbounded energy spreads, and any physical cutoff restores the cap. For photonic sensors, the information limit is set by photon dwell time.
AI.motivation: Non-Hermitian quantum sensing has been widely proposed as a route to dramatically enhanced precision via exceptional points and the skin effect, with some predicting exponentially large quantum Fisher information. However, whether this amplified response constitutes genuine measurement information has remained an open and unsettled question. This work aims to resolve this controversy.
AI.method: The authors prove a fundamental bound on quantum Fisher information for any open sensor where the parameter is imprinted coherently by a Hamiltonian, with loss, gain, non-reciprocity, and readout held fixed. They show the QFI is capped by the spread between the largest and smallest eigenvalues of the generator, independent of non-Hermitian dynamics. They also analyze the photon dwell-time formulation for photonic sensors.
AI.result: Non-Hermitian dynamics amplifies response but not information. Exponential gains require unbounded energy spreads; any finite photon-number cutoff restores the cap. The same limit governs dissipative probe preparation and spectral singularities. For photonic sensors, the QFI of any probe (classical or entangled) is set by the photon's dwell time at the perturbation.
AI.conclusion: Non-Hermiticity shapes a sensor's dynamics but does not source its precision. The generator's spread and the attainable dwell time serve as benchmarks for future non-Hermitian sensing proposals. The results contain recently derived scattering limits as special cases.

title: Phase-Programmable Free Electron Quantum States in Synthetic Momentum Space
summary: Light-electron interactions generate synthetic momentum-space dynamics that can be used to engineer free electron quantum states. Here we develop coherent control protocols in which the optical phase acts as the controllable hopping phase of a Floquet-Bloch momentum lattice. Pontryagin optimization designs phase-only waveforms that prepare selected momentum populations and coherent few-sideband superpositions with programmable relative phases. In a complementary Bragg regime protocol, dynamical phase matching selectively couples neighboring sidebands and enables deterministic sequential state synthesis. Full wave-packet simulations based on the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian identify the tolerance window set by phase noise, detuning, and finite momentum spread. The two protocols expose a speed-selectivity tradeoff between ultrafast multilevel interference control and slower resonant engineering, establishing programmable free electron sidebands as a platform for ultrafast quantum state synthesis.

AI.tldr: The paper develops two coherent control protocols (Pontryagin optimization and Bragg regime) for engineering free electron quantum states via optical phase-controlled Floquet-Bloch momentum lattices, demonstrating programmable sideband state synthesis with a speed-selectivity tradeoff.
AI.motivation: To establish programmable control over free electron quantum states using optical phase as a controllable hopping parameter in synthetic momentum-space dynamics, enabling ultrafast quantum state synthesis.
AI.method: Two protocols are developed: (1) Pontryagin optimization designs phase-only waveforms to prepare selected momentum populations and coherent few-sideband superpositions; (2) Bragg regime protocol uses dynamical phase matching to selectively couple neighboring sidebands for deterministic sequential state synthesis. Full wave-packet simulations based on the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian are used to evaluate robustness.
AI.result: Phase noise, detuning, and finite momentum spread tolerance windows are identified. The two protocols reveal a speed-selectivity tradeoff between ultrafast multilevel interference control (Pontryagin) and slower resonant engineering (Bragg regime).
AI.conclusion: Programmable free electron sidebands serve as a platform for ultrafast quantum state synthesis, with complementary protocols offering different tradeoffs in the speed-selectivity design space.

title: Turing mechanisms in a multimode open quantum system
summary: We investigate pattern formation in a finite chain of bosonic modes whose dynamics is governed by a Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad (GKSL) master equation. The model combines local parametric driving and nonlinear damping with nonlocal dissipative couplings between modes that work on different discrete spatial scales. In the classical limit, these mechanisms generate a reaction-diffusion-like dynamics, allowing the emergence of Turing-type instabilities. The key aspect of the analysis is the coexistence and competition of different unstable spatial modes. Depending on the range of parameters, the system may select different stationary nonuniform configurations, oscillatory wave-like states, or regimes in which multiple modes interact before a dominant pattern is established, thus providing a mechanism for pattern selection. We compare the deterministic bifurcation scenario, generated by a reaction-diffusion-like system derived from semiclassical drift dynamics, with the quantum dynamics, derived via the GKSL master equation, using phase-space methods and reduced Wigner functions. The results show how Turing instabilities, mode competition, and pattern selection can be extended to multimode open quantum systems, providing a bridge between nonlinear dynamical systems, dissipative quantum mechanics, and spatial self-organization.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Turing-type pattern formation in a finite chain of bosonic modes governed by a GKSL master equation, combining parametric driving, nonlinear damping, and nonlocal dissipative couplings. It demonstrates mode competition, pattern selection, and quantum-classical correspondence in dissipative quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To extend classical Turing instability theory and pattern formation mechanisms to multimode open quantum systems, bridging nonlinear dynamics, dissipative quantum mechanics, and spatial self-organization.
AI.method: The authors analyze a GKSL master equation for a bosonic chain with local parametric driving, nonlinear damping, and nonlocal dissipative couplings. They compare the deterministic semiclassical reaction-diffusion-like bifurcation analysis with full quantum dynamics using phase-space methods and reduced Wigner functions.
AI.result: The system exhibits Turing-type instabilities, coexistence and competition of multiple unstable spatial modes, leading to selection of stationary nonuniform configurations, oscillatory wave-like states, or regimes with dominant pattern emergence. Quantum and classical dynamics show correspondence.
AI.conclusion: Turing instabilities, mode competition, and pattern selection can be extended to multimode open quantum systems, establishing a bridge between classical nonlinear dynamics and dissipative quantum mechanics for spatial self-organization.

title: Spin Textures and Eigenstate Evolution of Isospectrally Patterned Lattices
summary: Isospectrally patterned lattices exhibit a composite band structure with a tunable ratio of localized versus delocalized eigenstates that is controlled by the underlying phase gradient. We show that the lattice Hamiltonian can be interpreted as that of a single spin exposed to a rotating magnetic field which is allowed to hop with a spin-flip across the lattice. In the low- and high-energy part of the band the localized states show an envelope of oscillatory character separated by quasi-nodes. Spin peaks occur at the locations of these quasi-nodes and provide a unique spin texture to the eigenstates which becomes increasingly complex with increasing degree of excitation. The crossover from localization to delocalization and vice versa leaves its fingerprints in the Fourier spectrum of the eigenstates: the original bimodal frequency distribution widens with increasing degree of excitation, moves across the spectral window and finally culminates in an extremely narrow frequency peak. In the course of this evolution the spin texture undergoes a rearrangement transition involving different characteristic (ir)regular patterns which we quantify by considering the total variation of the local spin fluctuations. Our results demonstrate the variety of the spectral properties of isospectrally patterned lattices which holds great prospect in particular when considering higher lattice or cell dimensions.

AI.tldr: Isospectrally patterned lattices exhibit tunable ratios of localized vs. delocalized eigenstates controlled by phase gradients. The system maps to a spin-hopping model with spin-flip interactions, producing oscillatory localized states with spin textures that reorganize as excitation increases, culminating in narrow frequency peaks.
AI.motivation: To understand the spectral properties and localization-delocalization transitions in isospectrally patterned lattices, which offer tunable control over eigenstate composition and hold promise for higher-dimensional applications.
AI.method: Hamiltonian mapping to a spin model under rotating magnetic field with spin-flip hopping; analysis of eigenstate envelopes, spin textures, Fourier spectra, and total variation of local spin fluctuations.
AI.result: Localized states exhibit oscillatory envelopes with quasi-nodes where spin peaks appear; crossover from localization to delocalization transforms bimodal frequency distributions into extremely narrow peaks; spin textures undergo rearrangement transitions with characteristic (ir)regular patterns.
AI.conclusion: Isospectrally patterned lattices display rich spectral diversity with tunable localization properties, promising for higher-dimensional lattice and cell configurations.

title: The NISQ Trap: Eight Years of Demonstrations the Hardware Was Built to Lose
summary: With a single contested exception, every NISQ-era flagship demonstration of "quantum advantage" has been classically reproduced, or closed by a simulability theorem, within eighteen months of its announcement. Six theoretical results from 2024 through April 2026 explain the pattern: the regions of circuit-space NISQ hardware can run with sufficient fidelity coincide with the regions classical algorithms compress efficiently, because the features that admit one (low effective depth, strong algebraic structure, geometric locality) are the features that admit the other. This reading dates the NISQ programme from its 2018 articulation as an interim retreat from the unmet conditions of the 1996 threshold theorems, characterises the eight years that followed as a closed loop in which the demonstrations the hardware could run were drawn from the only regions classical methods could already attack, and locates the exit from the loop where the threshold theorems originally located it: in fault tolerance. The empirical pattern could in principle break with a demonstration that escapes the current simulability results. After eight years and more than thirty advantage-class announcements, the burden of producing such a demonstration falls to the defenders of NISQ.

AI.tldr: Every NISQ-era quantum advantage claim has been classically reproduced within 18 months due to fundamental alignment between hardware-feasible circuits and classically simulable regions. This pattern dates from 2018 and suggests fault tolerance, not NISQ, is the correct path to quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: To explain why every NISQ-era quantum advantage demonstration has been classically reproduced within 18 months, and to argue that the NISQ programme has been a closed loop from 2018 to 2026 where hardware demonstrations only succeed in regions classical methods can already attack.
AI.method: Analysis of the pattern across all NISQ advantage claims; identification of six theoretical results (2024–April 2026) showing that circuit regions NISQ hardware can run with fidelity correspond exactly to regions classical algorithms can efficiently compress (due to shared features: low effective depth, strong algebraic structure, geometric locality).
AI.result: The regions of circuit-space accessible to NISQ hardware coincide with regions classically simulable; every advantage demonstration to date has been classically reproduced within 18 months; the NISQ programme (2018–2026) forms a closed loop.
AI.conclusion: The exit from the NISQ loop is located where the 1996 threshold theorems originally placed it: in fault tolerance. The burden of producing a non-simulable advantage demonstration now falls to NISQ proponents.

title: A Dynamic Multiplexing Policy for a Quantum Repeater
summary: We consider a multiplexed quantum repeater that distributes entanglement between two end nodes. Multiplexing is achieved through optical integration of many quantum chips. Each chip hosts an optically addressable communication qubit and a separate memory qubit. The communication qubit serves as an entanglement generation interface between different quantum chips, and the memory qubit can be used to store entanglement. The quantum chips on the repeater are interconnected using a reconfigurable router, which makes it possible to dynamically assign quantum chips for entanglement generation with either of the two end nodes in every end-to-end communication cycle. We propose a dynamic multiplexing policy in which after an entangled link has been established with one of the end nodes, all remaining quantum chips are assigned to the opposite end node. We compare this dynamic policy to a policy in which the assignment of quantum chips to end nodes is fixed. We consider a parameter regime where on average less than one entangled link is generated per end-to-end communication cycle, which is the relevant regime for near-term quantum networks. We show that in this regime, the dynamic multiplexing policy can lead to a significant improvement in fidelity over a fixed policy, while marginally improving the rate. Moreover, even though the dynamic multiplexing policy requires a deeper, and hence, more lossy, router than the fixed policy, it can still achieve higher secret key rates in the parameter regime studied. This makes dynamic multiplexing with a many-quantum-chip repeater especially relevant for the development of near-term quantum networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dynamic multiplexing policy for a multiplexed quantum repeater with multiple quantum chips (each containing a communication qubit and memory qubit) interconnected via a reconfigurable router. In this policy, after establishing an entangled link with one end node, all remaining chips are assigned to the opposite node. Compared to a fixed assignment policy, dynamic multiplexing significantly improves fidelity and marginally improves rate in the low-link regime (<1 link per cycle), achieving higher secret key rates despite requiring a deeper, lossier router. This is particularly relevant for near-term quantum networks.
AI.motivation: To improve entanglement distribution in near-term quantum networks where, on average, less than one entangled link is generated per end-to-end communication cycle—a regime where conventional fixed-assignment multiplexing is suboptimal.
AI.method: Proposes a dynamic multiplexing policy for a multiplexed quantum repeater architecture: multiple quantum chips (each with a communication qubit for entanglement generation and a memory qubit for storage) are interconnected via a reconfigurable optical router. After one entangled link is established with one end node, all remaining quantum chips are dynamically reassigned to the opposite end node. This is compared against a fixed-assignment policy.
AI.result: In the low-link regime (<1 link per cycle), the dynamic multiplexing policy yields significantly higher fidelity and marginally improved rate compared to the fixed policy. Despite requiring a deeper (more lossy) router, it achieves higher secret key rates.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic multiplexing with a many-quantum-chip repeater is especially advantageous for near-term quantum networks operating in the low-yield entanglement generation regime.

title: Towards Minimax Estimation of High-Order Functionals by Quantum Arguments
summary: We propose a novel approach to the minimax estimation of high-order functionals from the perspective of quantum computing. Specifically, for any real number $α\gg 1$, we present two estimators, one for the classical functional $\mathrm{F}_α(P) = \sum_{i=1}^S p_i^α$ of a discrete distribution $P$ and the other for the quantum functional $\mathrm{F}_α(ρ) = \operatorname{tr}(ρ^α)$ of a mixed state $ρ$. These functionals have close connections with the Rényi entropy and the Tsallis entropy. We show that both estimators achieve the minimax optimal $L_2$ rate $α\mathsf{n}^{-1}$ in the range $α\lesssim \mathsf{n} \lesssim α^{3-o(1)}$, where the support size $S$ of $P$ or the dimension of $ρ$ can be much larger than the number of samples $\mathsf{n}$. As a result, both estimators achieve the \textit{optimal} sample complexity $\mathsf{n} \asymp α$, improving upon the prior best upper bounds $O(α^2)$ established by Jiao, Venkat, Han, and Weissman (IEEE Trans. Inf. Theory 2017) for classical functionals and Chen and Wang (COLT 2025) for quantum functionals. Our estimators are constructed under a unified framework using quantum primitives and run in linear time on a quantum computer. This work reveals an unexpected path from quantum computing to statistics, suggesting a conceptually new methodology for functional estimation. It adds to the growing list of quantum proofs for classical theorems.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a quantum computing approach for minimax optimal estimation of high-order functionals (both classical and quantum), achieving optimal sample complexity n ≍ α, improving upon prior O(α²) bounds.
AI.motivation: Existing estimators for high-order functionals (Rényi/Tsallis entropy related) suffer suboptimal sample complexity O(α²). The authors aim to achieve the minimax optimal rate by leveraging quantum computing primitives.
AI.method: Two estimators are constructed under a unified quantum framework: one for classical functional F_α(P) = Σ p_i^α and another for quantum functional F_α(ρ) = tr(ρ^α). The estimators run in linear time on a quantum computer.
AI.result: Both estimators achieve the minimax optimal L₂ rate α n^{-1} in the range α ≲ n ≲ α^{3-o(1)}, with optimal sample complexity n ≍ α, improving upon prior best O(α²). Support size/dimension can be much larger than sample size.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computing provides a conceptually new methodology for functional estimation, revealing an unexpected path from quantum computing to statistics.

title: An analytical solution of a quantum system with non-Markovian behavior: The Bixon-Jortner system in time domain
summary: Non-Markovian behavior in quantum systems is often studied in the context of bipartite systems consisting of a system of interest and an environment -- tracing over the environment results in non-Markovian behavior for the subsystem of interest. One may get a Markovian limit in certain regimes, which is studied using the Lindblad master equation, and corrections to this behavior can be obtained by techniques such as the Nakajima-Zwanzig formalism. In this paper, we obtain an exact non-Markovian equation for the dynamics of a simple model system that consists of a direct sum rather than a tensor product of two pieces, namely, a discrete state and an infinite ladder. This system, called the Bixon-Jortner model, was first developed in the quantum chemistry literature but has been utilized by the quantum optics community as a model system with interesting behavior, including a Wigner-Weisskopf limit of exponential decay. We attack the time evolution problem of this system directly in time-domain, and start with an integrodifferential equation describing the time evolution of the discrete state. Using tools from mathematical physics, we transform this equation to a delay differential equation, which makes the non-Markovianity completely transparent, and then we solve the delay equation using an intuitive ansatz. This allows us to obtain the analytic form of the dynamics directly in time domain, and demonstrate decay and revival behaviors coming from the aforementioned delay differential equation. We believe the explicit form of the time-domain non-Markovian equation we obtain and the accessibility the solution techniques we use make our results a useful case study of non-Markovianity in quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The authors derive an exact non-Markovian equation for the Bixon-Jortner model (a direct-sum discrete state + infinite ladder system), transform the integrodifferential equation into a delay differential equation, solve it via ansatz, and analytically demonstrate decay and revival behaviors in the time domain.
AI.motivation: To obtain an exact, analytically solvable non-Markovian equation for a quantum system (Bixon-Jortner model) that goes beyond the typical tensor-product system-environment bipartite framework, and to make the non-Markovianity transparent through a delay differential equation formulation.
AI.method: The authors work directly in the time domain, starting with an integrodifferential equation for the discrete state. Using mathematical physics tools, they transform it into a delay differential equation. They solve the delay equation using an intuitive ansatz, yielding an explicit analytic form of the dynamics.
AI.result: An exact non-Markovian equation in time-domain is obtained for the Bixon-Jortner model. The delay differential equation makes non-Markovianity fully explicit, and the analytic solution reveals both decay and revival behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a clear, accessible case study of non-Markovianity in quantum systems, with explicit time-domain forms and solution techniques that can serve as a useful pedagogical and analytical tool.

title: Variational Learning with Sparse Long-range Entangling Gates
summary: The performance of variational quantum algorithms depends in general on the structure of the parametrized quantum circuit, but the most common ansätze are typically based on local couplings. Motivated by the extended connectivity available with neutral atoms and trapped ions, we examine when structured long-range connectivity provides a useful resource, focusing on sparse power-of-two (PWR2) coupling graphs. Using dynamical Lie-algebra analysis, approximate unitary-design diagnostics, and finite-depth measures of expressibility and entanglement, we examine how these geometries enlarge the accessible operator space. This enlarged space alone is not sufficient to ensure trainability of the parameterized circuit for given target problems, and we explore performance across example problems with and without long-range coupling, identifying where sparse coupling graphs are or are not likely to provide an advantage. We also introduce a variational scheme that maps hierarchical long-range Hamiltonians to geometrically local ones that can be optimized with short-range circuits. Together, these results identify circuit geometry and qubit reconfigurability as task-dependent resources for variational algorithms, relevant to ongoing developments in quantum hardware with long-range connectivity.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when structured long-range connectivity (specifically sparse power-of-two coupling graphs) in variational quantum algorithms provides advantages over local couplings, using dynamical Lie-algebra analysis, unitary-design diagnostics, and measures of expressibility/entanglement. It finds that enlarged operator space alone doesn't guarantee trainability, identifies problem-dependent benefits of long-range coupling, and introduces a variational scheme mapping hierarchical long-range Hamiltonians to local ones for short-range circuit optimization.
AI.motivation: To understand when structured long-range qubit connectivity (enabled by neutral atom and trapped ion platforms) provides a useful resource for variational quantum algorithms, given that most common ansätze rely on local couplings.
AI.method: Uses dynamical Lie-algebra analysis, approximate unitary-design diagnostics, finite-depth measures of expressibility and entanglement, and performance evaluation on example problems with and without long-range coupling.
AI.result: Structured long-range connectivity enlarges the accessible operator space, but this alone does not guarantee trainability; the advantage is problem-dependent. A variational scheme mapping hierarchical long-range Hamiltonians to local ones is introduced.
AI.conclusion: Circuit geometry and qubit reconfigurability are task-dependent resources for variational algorithms, with implications for quantum hardware development featuring long-range connectivity.

title: Control Protocols for Entangling Gates for Group-IV Color-Centers in Diamond
summary: Accurately controlling entangling gates remains a major challenge for quantum technology applications with solid-state spin qubits. Here, we study a group-IV color-center with a strongly-coupled nuclear spin and approach the problem from a quantum control perspective. We show that there are three different types of entangling gates where the entanglement is mediated by the parallel hyperfine-coupling component, the orthogonal one or both. We derive the respective quantum speed limits (QSL) and show by means of dynamical decoupling, resonant driving of single- and double-quantum transitions, quantum optimal control and algebraic gate decomposition how these gates can be realized. We finally discuss the experimental applicability.

AI.tldr: This paper studies entangling gates for solid-state spin qubits using a group-IV color-center with a strongly-coupled nuclear spin, identifying three types of entangling gates mediated by different hyperfine-coupling components, deriving their quantum speed limits, and presenting multiple control methods for realization.
AI.motivation: Accurately controlling entangling gates remains a major challenge for quantum technology applications with solid-state spin qubits.
AI.method: The authors study a group-IV color-center with a strongly-coupled nuclear spin from a quantum control perspective. They use dynamical decoupling, resonant driving of single- and double-quantum transitions, quantum optimal control, and algebraic gate decomposition to realize the gates.
AI.result: Three different types of entangling gates are identified, mediated by parallel hyperfine-coupling, orthogonal hyperfine-coupling, or both. Quantum speed limits (QSL) are derived for each gate type.
AI.conclusion: The experimental applicability of these entangling gate realizations is discussed.

title: RL-Guided Quantum-ALNS for Constrained VRP
comment: Funding source: Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council and Canada Research Chair
summary: This study develops a hybrid quantum-classical framework for constrained vehicle routing problems, focusing on the pickup-and-delivery problem with time windows. Instead of casting the full routing problem as a stand-alone quantum optimization task, we embed shallow quantum samplers inside the repair phase of an Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search (ALNS) heuristic. A Deep Q-Network controller decides whether each reduced repair subproblem should be handled by a classical repair heuristic or by a quantum sampler, using features that describe the local repair structure and predicted hardware reliability. IBM Heron experiments are used to calibrate an empirical noise-aware model for local quantum repair circuits. Across the tested instances, quantum repair is admissible in only about 16% of reduced repair states and is not superior on average. However, under selected matched repair budgets, quantum-enabled repair reduces the final gap relative to standard ALNS in 29 of 36 tested settings. These results suggest that near-term quantum sampling is most useful as a selective local repair mechanism rather than as a replacement for classical routing heuristics.

AI.tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical framework embeds shallow quantum samplers in the repair phase of ALNS for vehicle routing, guided by a DQN controller. Quantum repair, used in ~16% of cases, improves final gap in 29/36 settings under matched budgets, suggesting utility as a selective local repair mechanism rather than a full replacement.
AI.motivation: To explore whether near-term quantum computing can provide practical benefits for constrained vehicle routing problems without casting the entire problem as a stand-alone quantum optimization task.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical framework: shallow quantum samplers are embedded inside the repair phase of an Adaptive Large Neighbourhood Search (ALNS) heuristic, with a Deep Q-Network (DQN) controller deciding when to use classical vs. quantum repair. IBM Heron experiments calibrate an empirical noise-aware model for local quantum repair circuits.
AI.result: Quantum repair is admissible in only ~16% of reduced repair states and is not superior on average. However, under selected matched repair budgets, quantum-enabled repair reduces the final gap relative to standard ALNS in 29 of 36 tested settings.
AI.conclusion: Near-term quantum sampling is most useful as a selective local repair mechanism rather than as a replacement for classical routing heuristics.

title: RubriQ: Rubric-Guided Group Relative Policy Optimization for Constraint-Aware Quantum Circuit Synthesis
summary: Designing fault-tolerant quantum circuits that are both algorithmically correct and hardware compatible remains a major bottleneck in the transition to scalable quantum computing. We introduce RubriQ, a scalable framework that formulates circuit synthesis as a large language model (LLM) code-generation task, optimized via group relative policy optimization (GRPO). Unlike conventional black-box neural critics, RubriQ employs a domain-grounded programmatic rubric as the reinforcement learning reward function, evaluating circuits for T-gate reduction, hardware topology compliance, and unitary fidelity. To support high-throughput training, RubriQ integrates GPU-accelerated CUDA-Q simulation directly into the reinforcement learning (RL) loop and is deployed on NERSC Perlmutter using DeepSpeed ZeRO2 across multinode NVIDIA A100 clusters. On benchmark tasks, RubriQ achieves a mean T-gate compression of 3.31x, significantly outperforming sparse-reward RL baselines (2.05x), converging 2-3x faster, and maintaining less than 1\% hardware-constraint violations. Validated on IBM and IonQ quantum processors, RubriQ establishes an automated, high-performance computing (HPC)-driven pipeline for generating hardware-ready, fault-tolerant quantum circuits at scale.

AI.tldr: RubriQ is an HPC-driven framework that uses LLM code-generation optimized via GRPO with a domain-grounded rubric as the RL reward function, achieving 3.31x mean T-gate compression, 2-3x faster convergence, and <1% hardware-constraint violations on benchmark tasks, validated on IBM and IonQ processors.
AI.motivation: Designing fault-tolerant quantum circuits that are algorithmically correct and hardware compatible remains a major bottleneck in the transition to scalable quantum computing.
AI.method: Formulates circuit synthesis as an LLM code-generation task optimized via GRPO, using a domain-grounded programmatic rubric (evaluating T-gate reduction, topology compliance, unitary fidelity) as the RL reward function, with GPU-accelerated CUDA-Q simulation integrated into the RL loop and deployed on NERSC Perlmutter using DeepSpeed ZeRO2 across multinode NVIDIA A100 clusters.
AI.result: Mean T-gate compression of 3.31x (vs. 2.05x for sparse-reward RL baselines), 2-3x faster convergence, <1% hardware-constraint violations; validated on IBM and IonQ quantum processors.
AI.conclusion: RubriQ establishes an automated, HPC-driven pipeline for generating hardware-ready, fault-tolerant quantum circuits at scale.

title: Does Born Rule Imply Unitarity of Time Evolution in Quantum Mechanics?
summary: The Born rule for computing probabilities of the outcomes of measurements is an indispensable ingredient of quantum mechanics. The standard textbook description of this rule gives the impression that it implies the unitarity of time evolution. This view relies on the argument that unless the dynamics is unitary, the probabilities of finding all possible outcomes of a measurement do not add up to 1, i.e., the total probability is not conserved. We show that this argument is flawed, and that the general expression for the Born rule ensures the conservation of total probabilities even when the dynamics of a quantum system is not unitary. This applies to the dynamics of ensembles of quantum systems in both pure and mixed states. We discuss the status of the local conservation of probabilities and the arguments against the plausibility of non-unitary time evolutions that are based on the identification of the Hamiltonian operator with the energy observable.

AI.tldr: The Born rule conserves total probability even under non-unitary dynamics, challenging the standard view that unitarity is required for probability conservation.
AI.motivation: To correct the widespread misconception that the Born rule necessarily implies unitary time evolution, by showing that total probability conservation holds even for non-unitary dynamics.
AI.method: Logical analysis of the Born rule's mathematical structure, examining probability conservation under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics for pure and mixed states, and analyzing the role of the Hamiltonian as the energy observable.
AI.result: The Born rule generally ensures total probability conservation regardless of whether dynamics is unitary or not; the standard argument linking unitarity to probability conservation is flawed. Local probability conservation and the Hamiltonian-energy identification are examined as separate issues.
AI.conclusion: Non-unitary dynamics are not ruled out by probability conservation arguments based on the Born rule, suggesting that other criteria must be used to evaluate the plausibility of non-unitary time evolutions in quantum mechanics.

title: Relativistic Quantum Thermometry in AdS Spacetime via Non-Markovian Temperature Sensing
summary: Quantum thermometry based on single-qubit sensor configurations enables the precise estimation of the temperature of a cosmological Anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime. In this work, we characterize the achievable estimation accuracy using the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and the associated quantum signal-to-noise ratio. For the first time, we introduce an ancillary Unruh-DeWitt detector between the sensor and the thermal bath, enhancing thermometric sensitivity by channeling temperature-dependent information into the probe qubit's coherence. We examine how detector acceleration in AdS space and the choice of boundary conditions modify the probe's thermal sensitivity. Despite the differing geometries, a unified phenomenology emerges: we characterize the scaling of the QFI with respect to temperature, detector energy gap, spacetime curvature, and interaction time. Finally, we identify optimal state preparation and measurement strategies that maximize the QFI, thereby establishing the fundamental limits of precision for non-Markovian sensing in curved spacetime.

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes quantum thermometry precision for Anti-de Sitter spacetime using a single-qubit sensor, introduces an ancillary Unruh-DeWitt detector to enhance sensitivity, examines effects of detector acceleration and boundary conditions, and identifies optimal strategies maximizing Quantum Fisher Information for non-Markovian curved-spacetime sensing.
AI.motivation: To achieve precise temperature estimation of cosmological Anti-de Sitter spacetime and establish fundamental limits of quantum thermometry in curved spacetime environments.
AI.method: Using Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and quantum signal-to-noise ratio to characterize estimation accuracy; introducing an ancillary Unruh-DeWitt detector between sensor and thermal bath; analyzing detector acceleration in AdS space and boundary condition effects; identifying optimal state preparation and measurement strategies.
AI.result: Unified phenomenology emerges across differing geometries; scaling of QFI characterized with respect to temperature, detector energy gap, spacetime curvature, and interaction time; optimal state preparation and measurement strategies identified that maximize QFI.
AI.conclusion: Fundamental limits of precision for non-Markovian sensing in curved spacetime are established; ancillary Unruh-DeWitt detector enhances thermometric sensitivity by channeling temperature-dependent information into probe qubit coherence.

title: Analysis of the sample complexity for PAC-learning functions defined over quantum states
summary: A fundamental question in PAC learning is determining the number of labeled examples required to learn a concept class to a desired accuracy and confidence. In classical learning theory, this quantity is characterized by the VC-dimension, while several quantum generalizations have established analogous results when examples are provided in quantum superposition. In this work, we study a distinct quantum PAC-learning model in which concepts are functions acting on quantum states. We demonstrate that the VC-dimension, although still relevant, fails to fully capture the sample complexity of this model. To further characterize this setting, we develop a new lower bound on the required number of samples and establish an upper bound when the states in the domain are linearly independent. Remarkably, this upper bound has a form similar to the classical PAC-learning bound. We further examine a setting in which the learner receives more informative data and show that the limitations of the VC-dimension persist in this extended model.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a quantum PAC-learning model where concepts are functions on quantum states, showing VC-dimension fails to capture sample complexity, and develops new lower/upper bounds with an upper bound similar to classical PAC-learning when domain states are linearly independent.
AI.motivation: To determine the number of labeled examples required to learn a concept class in a distinct quantum PAC-learning model where concepts act on quantum states, and to understand whether classical measures like VC-dimension suffice.
AI.method: The paper analyzes sample complexity by developing a new lower bound and an upper bound for linearly independent domain states, and extends the investigation to a setting with more informative data.
AI.result: VC-dimension fails to fully capture sample complexity in this quantum model; a new lower bound is derived; an upper bound similar to classical PAC-learning is established for linearly independent states; limitations persist even with more informative data.
AI.conclusion: The VC-dimension is insufficient for this quantum PAC-learning model, and new sample complexity bounds are provided, with the linear independence case mirroring classical results.

title: Fidelity Analysis of Adiabatically Driven Donor Spins as Two-Qubit and Ququart Systems
summary: Donor spin systems host a native Hilbert space whose dimension exceeds that of a qubit, meaning they can be used as qudits. Here we study a \ce{Si{:}P} donor spin system through leakage-aware randomized benchmarking (RB) of native ququart $\mathcal{C}_4$ and encoded two-qubit $\mathcal{C}_2^{\otimes 2}$ Clifford groups. We implement adiabatic ramps to operate electron dipole spin resonance (EDSR) pulses at the ionization point, where the electron is shared halfway between the donor and the interface, and to operate electron spin resonance (ESR) pulses near the interface, motivated by the sensitivity of the effective magnetic field to charge noise at the ionization point. By placing the electron near the ionization point only during EDSR control and using sufficiently long displacement ramp durations, leakage outside the computational basis is strongly suppressed, which is crucial for optimized qudit control. We find in our analysis based on leakage RB that $\mathcal{C}_4$ consistently achieves $\sim 40$--$50\%$ lower (lower-bound) error rates $\varepsilon^{\mathrm{LB}}_\mathrm{PT}$ with respect to $\mathcal{C}_2^{\otimes 2}$, due to its reduced circuit complexity. These results indicate that donor spin qudits benefit from genuine qudit operation as opposed to imposed encoded qubit operation.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that native ququart (C4) operation on a Si:P donor spin system achieves 40-50% lower error rates compared to encoded two-qubit (C2⊗2) operation, as measured by leakage-aware randomized benchmarking, showing the advantage of genuine qudit control over encoded qubit approaches.
AI.motivation: Donor spin systems have native Hilbert space dimensions beyond qubits (qudits), but it was unclear whether operating them as genuine qudits offers advantages over encoding them as multiple qubits.
AI.method: Leakage-aware randomized benchmarking (RB) of native ququart C4 and encoded two-qubit C2⊗2 Clifford groups on a Si:P donor spin system; adiabatic ramps for EDSR pulses at the ionization point and ESR pulses near the interface; long displacement ramp durations to suppress leakage.
AI.result: C4 consistently achieves ~40-50% lower lower-bound error rates ε^LB_PT compared to C2⊗2 due to reduced circuit complexity.
AI.conclusion: Donor spin qudits benefit from genuine qudit operation rather than imposed encoded qubit operation.

title: Quantum Software Engineering in Practice: FPGA and AI Integration for Quantum Certification
summary: The emergence of Quantum Software Engineering (QSE) responds to the need for systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approaches to the development, operation, and maintenance of quantum software. Within this context, quantum computer certification represents a significant challenge: verifying that quantum devices produce valid entangled states despite hardware imperfections, noise, and decoherence. This paper presents QAccCert, a hybrid certification framework developed following QSE principles, demonstrating how heterogeneous technologies like FPGAs and Artificial Intelligence can be integrated for quantum processing. The framework implements entanglement certification through CHSH inequality violation in ideal quantum simulations using Qiskit AerSimulator. Through LLM-guided optimization, the system achieves 99.94% of the theoretical maximum of $2\sqrt{2}$, evidencing more efficient parameter space exploration than random search. These simulated results illustrate how QSE methodologies, combined with strategic technology interconnection, can be applied for practical and scalable quantum certification on real NISQ hardware in future work. This study provides a concrete case study of systematic quantum software development.

AI.tldr: QAccCert is a hybrid quantum certification framework developed using Quantum Software Engineering (QSE) principles, integrating FPGAs and AI (LLM-guided optimization) to certify quantum entanglement via CHSH inequality violation. In ideal simulations with Qiskit AerSimulator, it achieves 99.94% of the theoretical maximum (2√2), demonstrating efficient parameter optimization and providing a case study for systematic quantum software development targeting real NISQ hardware.
AI.motivation: The need for systematic, disciplined, and quantifiable approaches to quantum software development (Quantum Software Engineering), and the challenge of verifying that quantum devices produce valid entangled states despite hardware imperfections, noise, and decoherence.
AI.method: A hybrid certification framework (QAccCert) developed following QSE principles, integrating FPGAs and Artificial Intelligence. It implements entanglement certification through CHSH inequality violation in ideal quantum simulations using Qiskit AerSimulator, with LLM-guided optimization for parameter space exploration.
AI.result: The framework achieves 99.94% of the theoretical maximum of 2√2 through LLM-guided optimization, demonstrating more efficient parameter space exploration than random search.
AI.conclusion: QSE methodologies combined with strategic technology interconnection (FPGAs and AI) can be applied for practical and scalable quantum certification on real NISQ hardware in future work. The study provides a concrete case study of systematic quantum software development.

title: Operational Collapse Region in Repeaterless Loss-Dephasing Quantum Channels
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures. Presents initial findings on operational collapse regions where physical correlations persist
summary: The distribution of entangled photon pairs over standard optical fiber is a fundamental requirement for the realization of the quantum internet. However, real-world deployment is severely bottlenecked by the interplay of amplitude damping (photon loss) and phase noise (birefringence). In this paper, we numerically investigate the degradation of dual-rail polarization entanglement in telecom C-band fiber links. We demonstrate a critical disparity between the physical survival of quantum correlations and their practical utility in standard communication protocols. By evaluating the unconditional logarithmic negativity against the post-selected teleportation fidelity, we identify a distinct ``operational collapse region'' -- a distance window where the channel retains true quantum entanglement, yet standard coincidence-based detection architectures fail to provide any advantage over classical strategies. Furthermore, we reveal that the width of this inaccessible region exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the phase noise rate, implying that simply minimizing fiber dephasing does not necessarily optimize the operational efficiency of the network. These findings provide vital guidelines for the design of practical quantum communication links.

AI.tldr: This paper numerically studies dual-rail polarization entanglement degradation in telecom C-band fiber, revealing a critical "operational collapse region" where quantum entanglement exists but cannot be practically exploited for communication, and shows this region's width depends non-monotonically on phase noise rate.
AI.motivation: Distributing entangled photon pairs over standard optical fiber is essential for the quantum internet, but is severely bottlenecked by the combined effects of amplitude damping (photon loss) and phase noise (birefringence) in real-world deployments.
AI.method: Numerical investigation of dual-rail polarization entanglement degradation in telecom C-band fiber links; evaluation using unconditional logarithmic negativity and post-selected teleportation fidelity.
AI.result: Discovered a distinct "operational collapse region" where the channel retains true quantum entanglement but standard coincidence-based detection architectures provide no advantage over classical strategies. The width of this inaccessible region exhibits non-monotonic dependence on the phase noise rate.
AI.conclusion: Minimizing fiber dephasing does not necessarily optimize network operational efficiency; the findings provide guidelines for practical quantum communication link design.

title: Covariant Approximate Quantum Codes for Protected Analog Computation
summary: Quantum error correction compatible with continuous symmetries is a fundamental problem in quantum information and a possible route to robust analog quantum simulation. Because the Eastin-Knill theorem forbids exact codes with continuous transversal symmetries, we construct explicit $SU(d)$-covariant approximate codes that exploit permutation symmetry to spread logical information uniformly across all physical subsystems. For one-, two-, and three-qudit erasures at known locations, we prove worst-case purified-distance scaling $Θ(1/N)$, matching approximate Eastin-Knill lower bounds up to constants, and we extend the reduced-state analysis to general flagged local noise. For single-qudit erasure, we construct an explicit near-optimal decoder from the Petz recovery map. We then use these codes as building blocks for encoded analog dynamics. Symmetry-preserving Hamiltonians generate block-structured dynamical Lie algebras implementable transversally, while controlled symmetry-breaking terms serve as non-transversal resources for universal dynamics. These results provide explicit non-Abelian covariant codes and a framework for robust analog quantum simulation.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs explicit SU(d)-covariant approximate quantum error-correcting codes using permutation symmetry to distribute logical information uniformly, achieving optimal scaling for erasure errors, and uses these codes as building blocks for robust encoded analog quantum simulation with symmetry-preserving and symmetry-breaking terms.
AI.motivation: Quantum error correction compatible with continuous symmetries is a fundamental problem, but the Eastin-Knill theorem forbids exact codes with continuous transversal symmetries, motivating the construction of approximate codes that can bypass this limitation.
AI.method: The authors construct SU(d)-covariant approximate codes exploiting permutation symmetry, analyze worst-case purified-distance scaling for erasure errors, use Petz recovery map for optimal single-qudit erasure decoding, and utilize these as building blocks for encoded analog dynamics with block-structured dynamical Lie algebras.
AI.result: Proves worst-case purified-distance scaling Θ(1/N) for one-, two-, and three-qudit erasures, matching approximate Eastin-Knill lower bounds. Constructs explicit near-optimal decoder for single-qudit erasure via Petz recovery map.
AI.conclusion: Provides explicit non-Abelian covariant codes and a framework for robust encoded analog quantum simulation, using symmetry-preserving Hamiltonians for transversal implementation and controlled symmetry-breaking terms for universal dynamics.

title: Multi-stage Quantum Amplifier Readout Chain
summary: Multi-stage cryogenic readout chains with a wide bandwidth and added noise within a few quanta of the quantum limit are frequently constructed using traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) as the first stage, and a semiconductor amplifier as the second stage. Unfortunately for highly-scaled superconducting detector arrays, or quantum information systems, and space-based observatories, the power dissipation of the semiconductor amplifier becomes problematic from the perspective of available cryogenic cooling power at \mbox{3~K to 4~K}. Here we demonstrate a readout chain based on a two-stage kinetic inductance TWPA (KTWPA). This quantum-amplifier-based-readout-chain (QARC) provides sufficient gain that a cryogenic semiconductor follow-on amplifier can be eliminated without degradation of the system noise. In this way, the QARC dissipates approximately three orders of magnitude less power than readout chains containing semiconductor amplifiers while adding noise of less than 2~quanta over a 1~GHz bandwidth. In addition, by leveraging the high power handling of kinetic inductance technology, the QARC maintains an input compression point of -93~dBm, which exceeds that of many contemporary Josephson-junction-based parametric amplifiers.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a quantum-amplifier-based-readout-chain (QARC) using a two-stage kinetic inductance traveling-wave parametric amplifier (KTWPA) that eliminates the need for a cryogenic semiconductor follow-on amplifier, reducing power dissipation by ~1000x while maintaining <2 quanta added noise over 1 GHz bandwidth and a high input compression point of -93 dBm.
AI.motivation: The power dissipation of semiconductor amplifiers in multi-stage cryogenic readout chains is problematic for highly-scaled superconducting detector arrays, quantum information systems, and space-based observatories due to limited cryogenic cooling power at 3-4 K.
AI.method: A two-stage kinetic inductance traveling-wave parametric amplifier (KTWPA) is used to construct a quantum-amplifier-based-readout-chain (QARC) with sufficient gain to eliminate the need for a cryogenic semiconductor follow-on amplifier.
AI.result: The QARC dissipates ~1000x less power than chains with semiconductor amplifiers, adds <2 quanta noise over 1 GHz bandwidth, and maintains an input compression point of -93 dBm, exceeding many Josephson-junction-based parametric amplifiers.
AI.conclusion: A KTWPA-based readout chain can replace traditional semiconductor-based second-stage amplifiers, drastically reducing power consumption while preserving low-noise, high-bandwidth performance and high power handling capability.

title: Analysis of polarization drift of optical signals over deployed aerial-inground fiber connections
summary: Polarization measurements of a classical 1550-nm signal are collected and analyzed on 15-km hybrid aerial-inground fiber connections over 11 months. The spectral area and spectral moments9 of mHz-resolution Fast-Fourier-Transform (FFT) of these measurements are extracted, and related to temperature, humidity, wind speed, and time of day. Spectral area correlations show a strong11 diurnal structure: daytime maxima align with temperatures/wind speed peaks and humidity dips, with lower levels during the night. These diurnal patterns also show seasonality, with higher13 mean and variance in summer than winter. A random forest regressor is used to estimate FFT features from environmental measurements, informed by a theoretical model

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes polarization measurements of a 1550-nm signal over 11 months on 15-km hybrid aerial-inground fiber connections, extracting spectral features from mHz-resolution FFTs. It finds strong diurnal and seasonal correlations with environmental factors (temperature, humidity, wind speed) and uses a random forest regressor informed by a theoretical model to estimate FFT features from environmental measurements.
AI.motivation: To understand how environmental conditions affect polarization in hybrid aerial-inground fiber links over long timescales, which is important for polarization-sensitive communication systems.
AI.method: Polarization measurements of a 1550-nm signal were collected on 15-km hybrid aerial-inground fibers over 11 months. Spectral area and spectral moments were extracted from mHz-resolution FFTs. A random forest regressor, informed by a theoretical model, was used to estimate FFT features from environmental data.
AI.result: Spectral area correlations exhibit strong diurnal structure (daytime maxima aligned with temperature/wind peaks and humidity dips, lower at night). Diurnal patterns show seasonality with higher mean and variance in summer than winter.
AI.conclusion: Environmental factors strongly influence polarization dynamics in hybrid fiber links, and machine learning (random forest) combined with theoretical modeling can effectively estimate spectral features from environmental measurements.

title: QCNN with Rough Path Signature Kernels
summary: Time series analysis plays a vital role across a wide range of scientific and engineering domains but poses substantial computational challenges. A major difficulty arises from the time reparameterization invariance of time series data, which complicates the extraction of meaningful temporal features. In this work, we address the problem of time series classification by exploring the application of quantum computation techniques. We propose a hybrid quantum-classical architecture that integrates recent advances in quantum neural networks with the mathematical framework of path signatures, mitigating the impact of time reparametrization invariance. The architecture employs feature layers that compute a signature kernel between pairs of input paths, consisting of a reference path and a target path for classification, using either classical or quantum variational linear solvers (VQLS). These feature layers are followed by a Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) to perform downstream learning tasks. We evaluate several realizations of the proposed architecture, differing in QCNN configurations, on a binary classification task involving time series representations of handwritten digits. Our experiments demonstrate the potential advantages of implementing path signature kernel layers within quantum circuits and provide an analysis of the computational limitations associated with the VQLS component.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical architecture for time series classification that combines path signature kernels (to handle time reparameterization invariance) with Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks (QCNN), using either classical or variational quantum linear solvers (VQLS) for kernel computation, and demonstrates potential advantages on handwritten digit classification tasks.
AI.motivation: Time series classification faces computational challenges due to time reparameterization invariance, which complicates extraction of meaningful temporal features. The authors explore quantum computation techniques to address this problem more efficiently.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum-classical architecture that integrates: (1) feature layers computing a signature kernel between reference and target paths using classical or VQLS solvers, and (2) a Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) for downstream classification tasks.
AI.result: Experiments on binary classification of handwritten digit time series show potential advantages of implementing path signature kernel layers within quantum circuits, along with analysis of computational limitations of the VQLS component.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid quantum-classical architecture with path signature kernels and QCNN shows promise for time series classification, though the VQLS component introduces computational bottlenecks that need further optimization.

title: Faster quantum linear system solver beyond the condition number
summary: The spectral condition number is a widely adopted measure of worst-case cost for quantum linear system solvers. Yet it can significantly overestimate the actual runtime for a typical problem instance. We present two quantum algorithms that produce the normalized solution $|x\rangle$ of linear system $Ax=| b \rangle$ to accuracy $ε$ with complexity independent of the condition number $κ=\lVert A^{-1}\rVert$. We focus on the standard input model where $A$ is accessed through a block encoding and $| b \rangle$ is prepared by a unitary. But we also introduce an affine dilation model that encodes $A$ and $| b \rangle$ jointly, allowing further refinements of the query complexity. Our truncation-based solver makes an optimal number of queries to $| b \rangle$ and $\operatorname{\mathbf{O}}\left(κ_{\mathrm{eff}}\operatorname{polylog}\left(\frac{κ_{\mathrm{eff}}}ε\right)\right)$ queries to $A$. We prove a family of upper bounds on the effective condition number, including $κ_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq\frac{\lVert(A^\dagger A)^{-t/2}|x\rangle\rVert^{1/t}}{ε^{1/t}}$ for positive even integer $t$ and $κ_{\mathrm{eff}}\leq\frac{\lVert A^{-1\dagger}(A^\dagger A)^{-(t-1)/2}|x\rangle\rVert^{1/t}}{ε^{1/t}}$ for positive odd $t$, overcoming the $κ$-barrier. Our filtering-based solver is extremely simple with a favorable runtime prefactor. In particular, the solver has query complexity $6\frac{\lVert A^{-1\dagger}|x\rangle\rVert}ε\ln\left(\frac{1}ε\right)$ to leading order when the solution norm is known. We then present a similarly simple solution norm estimator with the same asymptotic cost up to logarithmic factors. Our quantum linear system solvers thus substantially improve a recent algorithm of Li, enabling faster quantum linear system solving beyond the condition number.

AI.tldr: Two quantum linear system solvers with complexity independent of the condition number κ, achieving query complexity O(κ_eff polylog(κ_eff/ε)) for the truncation-based solver and 6‖A^{-1†}|x⟩‖/ε ln(1/ε) for the filtering-based solver, overcoming the traditional κ-barrier.
AI.motivation: The spectral condition number κ can significantly overestimate the actual runtime of quantum linear system solvers for typical problem instances. The authors aim to design algorithms whose complexity is independent of κ, instead depending on a smaller "effective condition number" κ_eff that better captures instance-specific difficulty.
AI.method: Two algorithms: (1) A truncation-based solver with optimal queries to |b⟩ and O(κ_eff polylog(κ_eff/ε)) queries to A, using an affine dilation model. (2) A filtering-based solver with query complexity 6‖A^{-1†}|x⟩‖/ε ln(1/ε) to leading order, plus a similarly simple solution norm estimator.
AI.result: Proves upper bounds on κ_eff including κ_eff ≤ ‖(A†A)^{-t/2}|x⟩‖^{1/t}/ε^{1/t} for positive even t and κ_eff ≤ ‖A^{-1†}(A†A)^{-(t-1)/2}|x⟩‖^{1/t}/ε^{1/t} for positive odd t. The filtering-based solver has a favorable runtime prefactor and is simple to implement.
AI.conclusion: The proposed quantum linear system solvers substantially improve upon a recent algorithm by Li, enabling faster quantum linear system solving beyond the condition number barrier.

title: Multi-channel collective dissipation via the symmetric irreducible representation of SU(4)
summary: We specialize Agarwal's multi-level collective spontaneous-emission formalism to the four-level case by formulating it in the fully symmetric \SU(4) representation of $N$ identical atoms. In the irreducible representation $(N,0,0)$, the occupation-number basis forms a tetrahedral weight lattice on which the six embedded $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ transition subalgebras act as ladder operators. From these algebraic factors we obtain a compact Pauli-type population-rate equation and a closed-form expression for the total emitted intensity that apply to any combination of open dipole channels. The formalism is then specialized to the seven dipole-allowed four-level topologies -- tripod, inverted tripod, Y, inverted Y, double-$Λ$, closed cascade, and diamond -- and the resulting rate equations are solved numerically for atom numbers up to $N=50$. In every case the emitted intensity develops a delayed cooperative burst whose peak height obeys a power law $I_{\mathrm{peak}}=aN^{p}$ with topology-dependent parameters $(a,p)$; the fitted exponents lie in the range $1.81\lesssim p\lesssim 1.92$, indicating a superlinear. The \SU(4) tetrahedral flow and the seven configuration-dependent transients together provide a unified geometric picture of multi-channel collective dissipation in four-level atomic ensembles.

AI.tldr: This paper extends collective spontaneous-emission theory to four-level atomic systems using SU(4) symmetry, deriving rate equations for seven dipole-allowed topologies and finding that cooperative bursts follow a superlinear power law (p~1.81-1.92) with topology-dependent parameters.
AI.motivation: To generalize multi-level collective emission formalism (previously specialized to two- and three-level systems) to four-level atomic ensembles, enabling study of cooperative effects in richer level structures.
AI.method: Formulates the problem in the fully symmetric SU(4) irreducible representation (N,0,0), uses occupation-number basis on a tetrahedral weight lattice with six embedded su(2) transition subalgebras, derives compact Pauli-type population-rate equations, and solves numerically for N up to 50 across seven dipole-allowed topologies.
AI.result: All seven topologies exhibit delayed cooperative bursts with superlinear peak intensity scaling I_peak = a N^p, where p ranges from ~1.81 to 1.92 with topology-dependent prefactors.
AI.conclusion: The SU(4) tetrahedral flow and topology-dependent transients provide a unified geometric description of multi-channel collective dissipation in four-level systems.
